AI is the main growth driver, but technology shifts can reshuffle winners. Dell'Oro sees Ethernet gaining against Nvidia's InfiniBand and NVLink in scale-up, and 1.6 Tbps switches ramping at least five times faster than 800 Gbps. Vendors that miss a transition lose share.

Demographics matter little directly. Population and workforce trends influence carrier subscriber growth and public-safety budgets only slowly. We found no sourced evidence of a demographic effect on this sub-industry.

Consumer and enterprise behaviour shows in Wi-Fi and campus refresh: Cisco said Wi-Fi 7 was over 50% of wireless orders in Q4. Carriers' data demand growth has not turned into higher RAN spending, with the market flat.

New competitors and business models include white-box switch makers, Nvidia's networking, and silicon vendors. Dell'Oro lists Celestica and Nvidia ahead of Arista in Ethernet AI back-end sales. Cisco's rise to fourth shows share can move quickly.

Geopolitics and supply chains are important: Dell'Oro expects supply constraints for one to two years, and Ericsson flags rising component costs. Cisco's filing cites international and geopolitical risks. Customer concentration at Ciena makes loss of a top buyer significant.

Substitutes include in-house cloud networking by hyperscalers and cheaper alternatives to carrier-grade equipment. Meta, Microsoft and others partner on Arista's Etherlink SU-144 design, showing customers shape products. We found no source sizing substitution risk.
AI back-end switch spending is forecast to approach $1 trillion cumulatively over 2026-2030, with scale-up above half of the market by 2030.
Nokia's IP Networks sales grew 45% and Optical 19% in Q3 2026 on AI and cloud demand.
Cisco guides to $72.2-73.4 billion of fiscal 2027 revenue, up from $63.3 billion.
Alphabet and Amazon both said they expect higher capex in 2027.
Hyperscaler budgets may flatten; Microsoft lowered its 2026 forecast on third-party data-centre delays.
Rising component costs and mix dilute gross margins, as flagged by Arista and Ericsson.
Concentrated customers can cut orders quickly: two customers were 41.7% of Ciena's revenue.
Mobile equipment stays flat, limiting growth at Ericsson.

Over three to five years, we think the sub-industry's results are set by whether the AI networking build continues at the pace implied by Dell'Oro's forecast and hyperscaler guidance. The evidence for the next year or two is strong: orders, backlogs and guidance are rising, and supply, not demand, is the limit. The risks are about margin and durability. Mix and component costs are already trimming gross margins, valuation data from January 2026 sit well above the market, and the AI exposure is concentrated in a few buyers. Carrier equipment is likely to remain a slow, flat business, with Motorola's public-safety backlog providing steadier growth. Our read is that growth stays high while margins plateau, rather than a collapse or an unbroken climb.

This sub-industry is moving with a capex cycle rather than the consumer economy. The S&P 500 is in a strong earnings period, with blended third-quarter earnings growth of 30.2% and revenue growth of 13.4% as of 30 October 2026. The forward P/E of 18.7 is below its five-year average of 19.8. Within that, the key variable for equipment makers is spending by five large cloud and AI builders, forecast at $803-828 billion for 2026 and rising from $188.5 billion in Q2 to about $227 billion in Q3.

Not all of the group rides that cycle. Ericsson describes the RAN market as flat and expects component costs to weigh on 2027 gross margin. Nokia keeps its 2026 comparable operating profit target of EUR 2.1-2.6 billion while its Fixed Networks sales fell 21% and AI and Cloud sales rose 126%. Public-safety demand shows up in Motorola's record $16.6 billion backlog. We did not find a source tying interest rates or currency to this sub-industry's results, so we do not make a claim there. Our read is that the cycle is late-expansion for AI networking and flat for telecom.

The structural driver is AI. Dell'Oro's July 2026 forecast has cumulative AI back-end switch spending approaching $1 trillion over 2026-2030, with scale-up networking more than half of the market by 2030 and 1.6 Tbps ramping at least five times faster than 800 Gbps. In Q2 2026, AI back-end switch sales passed front-end switch sales for the first time. Cisco's hyperscale AI orders were $9.3 billion in fiscal 2026, about 4.5 times fiscal 2025.

Demand is cyclical because it depends on a few buyers. The combined 2026 capex forecast is $803-828 billion, and Alphabet and Amazon said they expect to spend more in 2027, while Meta's plans are still being drawn up and Microsoft cut its 2026 estimate on data-centre delays. Nokia's IP Networks grew 45% and Optical 19% in Q3 2026. Outside AI, demand is steadier: carrier RAN is flat, while enterprise Wi-Fi refresh is helped by Wi-Fi 7, over half of Cisco's Q4 wireless orders. Demographics matter little here.

Porter's five forces point to a sub-industry with strong rivalry but high barriers. Threat of new entrants is low in carrier-grade and data-centre gear because silicon, software and customer qualification take years, but new-model entrants matter: Dell'Oro ranks Celestica first and Nvidia second in Ethernet AI back-end switching, ahead of Arista third and Cisco fourth, which made the biggest share gain. Rivalry is intense; Cisco's filing names Arista, Broadcom, Ciena, Dell, HPE, Huawei, Nokia and Nvidia as competitors.

Buyer power is high: Arista's dependence on large clouds and their negotiating power is a flagged risk, and two customers were 41.7% of Ciena's revenue. Supplier power is rising as memory, chips and optics tighten; Dell'Oro expects supply constraints for one to two years and Ericsson sees higher component costs in 2027. The threat of substitutes comes from hyperscalers' own designs and Nvidia's proprietary links; Dell'Oro expects Ethernet to become the leading scale-up technology by 2030. Moats are software (Arista's EOS), silicon (Cisco Silicon One) and installed base; the sourced evidence is margin: Arista 64.0% gross, Cisco 66.3%.

Political and regulatory factors we could source are limited. Cisco's 10-K lists regulation of AI, privacy and cybersecurity, international and geopolitical conditions and currency among its risk factors. We did not locate current sources on export controls, tariffs or telecom spectrum policy for this group, so we make no claim about them.

Technology is the largest force. Ethernet has extended its lead in AI back-end networks, 800 Gbps switches account for most Ethernet AI back-end revenue and 1.6 Tbps switches have begun sampling. Scale-up networking, currently dominated by Nvidia's NVLink, is expected to open to Ethernet and UALink. Cisco shipped more than 75,000 800G coherent pluggables in fiscal 2026 and says three hyperscalers use its P200 platform for scale-across networks. Arista introduced its Etherlink SU-144 design in October. Economic factors include component and memory availability. Social and environmental factors, such as power use of AI sites, were not covered by sources we opened.

Margins differ widely by business model. Non-GAAP operating margin was 49.1% at Arista, 35.9% at Cisco in its July 2026 quarter, 32.5% at Motorola Solutions, 22.5% at Ciena and 22.0% for HPE Networking. Ericsson's adjusted EBITA margin was 17.0%, down from 28.1% a year before, which included a large capital gain. Nokia's comparable operating margin was 11.7%. Damodaran's January 2026 industry table shows a 20.53% after-tax operating margin and 52.73% return on invested capital for 57 telecom-equipment firms, against 11.88% and 9.76% for the market.

Gross-margin direction is mixed. Ciena's non-GAAP gross margin rose to 46.4% from 41.9% while Cisco's non-GAAP fell to 66.3% from 68.4%, Arista's to 64.0% from 65.2% and Ericsson's adjusted gross margin was 47.7% versus 48.1%. Balance sheets are strong: Arista has about $14.4 billion in cash and securities, Ericsson net cash of SEK 60.7 billion. Cisco's fiscal 2026 operating cash flow was $14.2 billion, flat. Capital intensity is low, as Ciena's nine-month equipment purchases were $194.9 million.

Company guidance is the best evidence we have; we did not find sub-industry consensus estimates. FactSet's S&P 500 data show Q4 2026 earnings growth expected at 28.4% and calendar 2026 at 32.9%, but it gives no figure for this sub-industry. Cisco guides fiscal 2027 revenue to $72.2-73.4 billion and non-GAAP EPS to $5.05-5.11, against $4.33 in fiscal 2026. Arista guides Q4 revenue to $3.9-4.0 billion with a 48-49% non-GAAP operating margin and EPS of $1.26-1.30. Ciena guides fiscal 2026 revenue to $6.42 billion and Q4 to $1.75 billion. Motorola raised full-year non-GAAP EPS to $17.94-17.99. Nokia sees Q4 revenue up 20-24% sequentially and 2026 comparable operating profit of EUR 2.1-2.6 billion.

Our read is that the revisions are positive for AI networking: Arista's Q4 guide was above the roughly $3.6 billion analysts expected, and Nokia's AI and Cloud orders rose 118%. The difference from a simple extrapolation is gross margin, where mix and component costs are working against growth. Ericsson's flat RAN outlook is the main drag in the group.

We have no sourced current multiple for the sub-industry. The best reference is Damodaran's January 2026 dataset, now ten months old, which shows a forward P/E of 39.47 for 57 Telecom. Equipment firms against 27.66 for the total market, a trailing P/E of 84.72, and a PEG ratio of 0.87 against 1.90. On enterprise value, EV/EBITDA is 24.07 versus 19.73 for the market for positive-EBITDA firms, and EV/EBIT is 30.86 versus 29.12. The S&P 500 forward P/E was 18.7 on 30 October 2026, under its five-year average of 19.8.

Read together, we think the group was priced at a premium to the market on earnings but nearer parity on a growth-adjusted basis in January, which fits the PEG ratio. Since then, estimates for AI networking names have moved up, and Arista's shares were about 25% below their all-time high at about $180 after its November results. We did not find a current free-cash-flow yield for the group, and these January figures should be treated as stale for individual stocks.

We found no sourced short-interest, fund-flow or breadth data for this sub-industry, so this section is limited to what the opened ETF page shows. The iShares U.S. Telecommunications ETF (IYZ), which holds communications-equipment names alongside carriers, had $701 million of assets and 26 holdings in its page updated 5 November 2026. Its top weights were Cisco at 22.90%, Verizon 12.32%, Arista 10.63%, AT&T 4.54% and Motorola Solutions 4.52%, with the top ten at 73.02%. That shows how concentrated exposure to this group is in a handful of names.

Price momentum is mixed in what we saw. Arista rose about 6% after its results but closed below its 200-day average and about 25% below its all-time high, per XTB. Hyperscaler capex data and Dell'Oro's supply-constraint view argue that fundamentals are still ahead of positioning, but we cannot back that with flow data. Readers should check current ETF holdings and prices before relying on any weight here.

IT Consulting & Other Services is growing slowly while investors argue about whether AI shrinks the work. Accenture grew fiscal 2026 revenue 6% to $74.2 billion and guided fiscal 2027 to 3% to 6% local-currency growth; Cognizant guides 2026 to 4.0% to 4.4% constant-currency growth; Infosys cut its FY27 guide to 1% to 2%; EPAM guided Q4 revenue roughly flat year on year. Accenture rose about 22% on 1 October after falling about a third earlier in 2026. In July, Pzena put Accenture at 8.7x forward earnings against a 5-year median of 24.3x. Sub-industry consensus and ETF flow data were not publicly available to us.

These companies sell skilled people and know-how. Clients such as banks, insurers, manufacturers and governments hire them to design and build software, connect old and new systems, run IT operations and business processes, and advise on strategy. Revenue mostly comes from billing for time, or from fixed-price and multi-year contracts. Costs are mainly salaries, so size, utilisation and offshore delivery in India and elsewhere matter. GICS places IT consulting, systems integration and outsourcing here. Software makers, data-processing firms and cloud hosts sit in neighbouring sub-industries.
Consulting and strategy: Advice on how to use technology, data and AI to change a business, usually sold in short projects. e.g. Accenture Strategy, Cognizant Consulting, Capgemini Invent

Systems integration and application development: Building, customising and connecting software such as SAP, Salesforce or cloud platforms so they work with a client's existing systems. e.g. Accenture, Infosys, EPAM, Globant

Managed services and outsourcing: Running a client's IT infrastructure, applications or business processes for several years under contract, with a service level promised. e.g. Accenture Managed Services, Cognizant, IBM Consulting
Digital engineering and product development: Engineering teams that build software products for clients, including technology companies. e.g. EPAM, Globant
Industry platforms: Software or platforms owned by the services firm and run for clients, which earn recurring fees. e.g. Cognizant TriZetto healthcare platform
AI and data services: Preparing data, building and deploying AI applications and agents, and training client staff to use them. e.g. Accenture, Infosys, Cognizant AI offerings

Corporate technology budgets: Clients spend on IT projects when profits and confidence are good. In weak periods discretionary consulting is cut first, while multi-year managed services hold up better.
AI and pricing: AI can cut the hours needed for coding and testing. If clients demand lower prices, revenue per project falls; if cheaper work lets clients do more projects, volume can offset it.
Utilisation, attrition and wage inflation: Salaries are the main cost. Rising pay or high attrition squeezes margins unless prices rise, and idle staff cost money.
Mix of contracts: Fixed-price and outcome-based deals can earn higher margins when delivery is efficient, but add risk. Managed services add stability.
Acquisitions: Large firms buy specialist companies to add skills and clients. This lifts reported growth but adds integration risk and goodwill.
Currency and offshore costs: Revenue is mostly in dollars and euros while many staff are paid in rupees or other currencies, so exchange rates move margins.
Bookings: The total value of new contracts signed in a period. It is the main forward indicator, because it turns into revenue over months or years.
Book-to-bill: Bookings divided by revenue for the same period. Above 1.0 means the order book is growing.
Time-and-materials: Billing clients by the hour or day. Revenue tracks headcount, so productivity gains from AI can reduce revenue unless pricing changes.
Fixed-price / outcome-based: The client pays an agreed sum for a deliverable or result. The vendor keeps productivity gains but carries the risk of overruns.
Managed services: Multi-year contracts to run systems or processes. Revenue is steadier than consulting, which clients can cut in a few weeks.
Utilisation: The share of billable staff time that is actually billed. Low utilisation means paying salaries without revenue.
Offshore pyramid: A staffing model with many junior staff in lower-cost locations, supervised by fewer senior people. AI threatens the junior base.
Attrition: The rate at which staff leave. High attrition raises hiring and training costs and can hurt project quality.
Revenue per employee: Revenue divided by headcount. A quick gauge of pricing and productivity; it can rise if AI lets fewer people deliver the same work.
Constant currency: Growth with exchange-rate changes stripped out. Services firms with global clients and costs in other currencies report it alongside US dollar growth.
Large deal / TCV: A contract above a size threshold, with total contract value (TCV) counting its whole life. Companies disclose them to show momentum.
Global capability centre (GCC): A client's own offshore technology centre. Growth in GCCs lets clients do in-house some work they once outsourced.
Whether clients keep demanding a share of AI savings: Accenture said pricing was lower in many areas in Q4, and Infosys lowered its growth range.
Q1 bookings and book-to-bill at Accenture, which will show whether the October rebound rests on real demand; Cognizant's Q3 bookings fell 7%.
Fixed-price and outcome-based contracts, which analysts say decide whether productivity gains are kept by vendors or passed to clients.
Policy uncertainty, oil prices and supply-chain disruption delaying decisions in two Cognizant client sectors.
Share price behaviour after the October squeeze: in June Accenture fell about 18% in a day on a cautious outlook.
Accenture, Cognizant, Infosys, EPAM Systems, IBM, Capgemini, Globant

Revenue comes from consulting projects, systems integration and long-running managed services. Accenture splits its revenue between Consulting and Managed Services, which were $9.28 billion and $9.40 billion in Q4 FY26. Fees are billed per hour, at fixed prices or on outcomes.

Customers are large corporations and governments across industries. Accenture serves more than 9,000 clients; US federal work was about 7% of its fiscal 2026 revenue. Cognizant draws roughly 60% of revenue from healthcare and financial services.

People are the main cost. Accenture had about 814,000 employees at 31 August 2026, mostly in India, the Philippines and the US. Its SG&A was 16.3% of FY26 revenue, so delivery staff cost is the larger piece.

Pricing power rests on trust, scale, industry knowledge and being embedded in clients' systems. Accenture says clients retain it on a non-exclusive basis, and consulting contracts can be ended on about 30 days' notice, which limits pricing power in advisory work.

Main assets are people, client relationships, acquired businesses and cash. Accenture held $12.8 billion of cash and $10.0 billion of long-term debt at 31 August 2026. Cognizant held $1.52 billion of cash against $1.55 billion of long-term debt at the end of Q3 2026.
The model is asset-light. There are few factories or networks, and spending goes mostly on staff, training and acquisitions. Accenture spent $4.9 billion on 17 acquisitions in fiscal 2026.

Gartner forecasts worldwide IT spending of $6.31 trillion in 2026, up 13.5%, with IT services the largest category. The republished release prints the services figure as $1.87 billion, which is a unit slip, and we could not confirm its growth rate, so we treat it as roughly $1.9 trillion. It is wider than this sub-industry. Pzena puts IT services at about 30% of global technology spending.

The main segments are consulting, systems integration, application development and maintenance, and infrastructure or business process outsourcing. Accenture reports Consulting and Managed Services; Cognizant reports by client industry, such as Financial Services and Health Sciences.

Services sit between technology suppliers (cloud, software and hardware vendors) and corporate customers. The firms implement SAP, Salesforce, Microsoft and cloud systems and run them for clients, so they depend on the spending decisions of both sides.

The industry grew from outsourcing and offshoring in the 1990s and 2000s into cloud, digital and now AI work. Accenture says it has invested $3.0 billion in AI over three years and counted nearly 110,000 AI and data practitioners at year end.

Delivery is concentrated in India, with large presences in the Philippines, Eastern Europe and Latin America, while demand is concentrated in North America and Europe. Accenture's Americas revenue was $9.43 billion in Q4 FY26 against $6.58 billion in EMEA and $2.67 billion in Asia Pacific.

There are hundreds of significant competitors worldwide. Accenture's 10-K names categories rather than firms: large multinational IT providers, offshore providers in India, accounting firms and consultancies, niche specialists and clients' own IT departments.

Accenture is the largest listed player at $74.2 billion of fiscal 2026 revenue. Cognizant guides 2026 revenue at about $22.1 billion. Infosys booked half-year revenue of Rs 97,454 crore. EPAM's Q3 revenue was $1.43 billion. We did not find a sourced market-share table.
The industry is fragmented. A few giants lead, but the long tail of regional and specialist firms is large, and acquisitions continue: Accenture alone bought 17 companies in fiscal 2026.

Barriers to entry are modest for a small consulting shop, since the main input is people. They are high for large managed-services deals, which need references, security credentials, global delivery and balance-sheet strength.

Economies of scale exist in recruiting, training, offshore delivery and partnerships. Accenture's revenue per employee is about $90,000, nearly twice India's largest outsourcers, which Pzena reads as evidence of mix and pricing advantage.

Work is partly commoditised. Basic coding, testing and support are increasingly benchmarked on price, while advisory and complex integration are more differentiated. Accenture says 'AI-native companies' are among its competitors.

Customers hold much of the bargaining power in routine work: contracts can be rebid, and renewal price step-downs have moved from 3% to 4% to roughly 6% to 7%, per Pzena. Suppliers are mainly employees, so wage inflation and talent scarcity are the supplier pressure.

Revenue growth is driven by client technology budgets, new bookings, price per unit of work and acquisitions. Accenture's Q4 book-to-bill was 1.2 overall, but only 1.0 in Consulting against 1.4 in Managed Services.

Operating margin depends on pricing, utilisation, the share of offshore staff, attrition, and the mix of contracts. Accenture's adjusted operating margin was 15.8% for FY26 and it guides to 50 to 70 basis points of GAAP expansion in FY27.
The key cost variables are salaries, hiring and training, subcontractors, and acquisition integration. Accenture says it spent about $1.0 billion on learning and development in fiscal 2026.

Interest-rate sensitivity is indirect and moderate. Higher rates raise financing costs for clients and delay projects, but the firms themselves carry little debt, so earnings are barely touched directly. Accenture issued about $5.0 billion of net debt in fiscal 2026. We found no sourced rate-sensitivity estimate.

Inflation lifts wages and pushes costs up, but contract repricing can lag. GDP and corporate profits drive discretionary spending; Cognizant attributed its lower outlook to policy uncertainty, oil prices and supply-chain disruptions delaying decisions. Commodity prices matter mainly through client industries such as energy.

The industry is cyclical in consulting but defensive in managed services, with a structural AI and cloud tailwind that is now contested. Accenture's Consulting book-to-bill was only 1.0 while Managed Services was 1.4. Pzena notes that IT services stocks trade as if the structural story is in doubt.

Growth has slowed to low-to-mid single digits. Accenture grew 5% in local currency in fiscal 2026 and guides 3% to 6% for FY27; Cognizant guides 4.0% to 4.4%; Infosys guides 1% to 2%; EPAM grew 2.3% in Q3.

Damodaran's January 2026 data for 64 US Computer Services firms show a gross margin of 24.3%, a net margin of 4.5% and a pre-tax operating margin of 7.4%. Large leaders earn far more: Accenture 15.8% adjusted, Cognizant 16.3% adjusted in Q3, EPAM 16.7% non-GAAP, and Infosys 21% in Q2 FY27. The group figure includes smaller, lower-margin firms.

Returns are very high because the business needs little capital. Damodaran's normalised ROIC for the US Computer Services group is 37.4%, and after-tax ROIC unadjusted is 39.3%. The page's date labels conflict (January 2026 versus January 2025), so treat these as indicative.

Leverage is low. Accenture held $12.8 billion of cash against $10.0 billion of long-term debt, while Cognizant's long-term debt rose to $1.55 billion after drawing $1.0 billion on its revolver, against $1.52 billion of cash.

Free cash flow is strong. Accenture generated $11.6 billion in fiscal 2026, about 16% of revenue, and Cognizant generated $925 million in Q3, about 16% of revenue. Pzena says the group converts 90% or more of earnings into cash.

Capital expenditure is small relative to cash flow; the main uses of cash are acquisitions and buybacks. Accenture returned a record $11.5 billion to shareholders and spent $4.9 billion on acquisitions. Cognizant spent $1.88 billion on buybacks year to date.

Damodaran's January 2026 US Computer Services group trades at 14.1x EV/EBITDA (positive-EBITDA firms) and 19.3x EV/EBIT. Leaders trade lower on forward earnings: Pzena had Accenture at 8.7x and Cognizant at 6.7x on 30 June 2026.

Regulation and legislation: visa costs for H-1B and similar visas, trade restrictions and tariffs are named risks in Accenture's 10-K. Data-protection and AI rules add compliance costs. We found no single pending law that changes the sub-industry's economics.

AI is the central risk. Accenture warns that work 'has been and will continue to be replaced by automation, including AI-enabled solutions', which 'has led and may continue to lead to reduced demand'. ICICI Securities estimates a 10% to 20% deflationary effect at contract renewals, offset by new AI workloads.

Demographics matter through talent supply and offshore wage inflation. Infosys's voluntary attrition eased to 12.7% from 14.3% a year earlier, and its headcount was 332,542. An ageing workforce and skills shifts are slower-moving pressures that we did not find quantified.

Changing client behaviour: clients are building in-house teams, including global capability centres, and shifting budgets toward AI investments, which the 10-K lists as competition and as a budget risk. Phil Fersht of HFS says demand is moving to focused AI work while large transformation projects stay under pressure.

New competitors and models include AI-native firms and software platforms. Palantir said its offerings compress SAP migration timelines from years to weeks, and Anthropic launched plug-ins that automate legal, sales and data work, per Business Today. Accenture and Anthropic each committed at least $1 billion over five years to a partnership, showing incumbents are also partnering.

Geopolitical risk is mostly about delivery locations and trade policy. Cognizant cited oil prices and supply-chain disruption delaying decisions; Accenture's 10-K names tariffs and trade restrictions. Concentration of staff in India and the Philippines is a further exposure.

Substitutes include in-house teams, software with built-in AI, and clients simply buying less. Pzena argues disintermediation is limited because clients want to avoid managing non-core transformation and AI start-ups lack embedded relationships. We think the risk is real but the pace is uncertain.
Clients need partners to prepare data, integrate AI into core systems and govern it; Infosys reported AI services at 10.5% of revenue, up 29% sequentially.
Lower unit costs can make more backlog worth doing, so volume could offset price falls, as Pzena argues.
Shifting to fixed-price and outcome-based contracts lets vendors keep productivity gains.
Acquisitions and managed-services demand continue: Accenture expects roughly $5 billion of acquisitions in fiscal 2027 and had $12.77 billion of Q4 managed-services bookings.
AI-led deflation at renewals could cut revenue faster than new work arrives, as ICICI Securities estimates.
AI-native competitors and in-house capability centres could take routine work and weaken pricing.
Cognizant's 7% fall in Q3 bookings and Infosys's guidance cut suggest decisions are being delayed.
Visa and tariff changes could raise delivery costs.

Our read is that the next three to five years bring low-to-mid single-digit industry growth, with a widening gap between leaders and the rest. Leaders such as Accenture have scale, balance sheets and bookings (141 deals of $100 million or more in a quarter), while pricing is clearly softer. Whether volume offsets deflation will show up in bookings, revenue per employee and operating margins over several quarters. Guidance from Cognizant and Infosys shows demand is not recovering evenly. We see the sector as a transition story in which margins held so far, but growth rates are low and the distribution of outcomes is wide.

IT services follows corporate confidence more than consumer demand. Cognizant guided 2026 growth of 4.0% to 4.4% in constant currency and blamed policy uncertainty, oil prices and supply-chain disruption for decision delays in two client sectors. Infosys also lowered its FY27 guide to 1% to 2% from 1.5% to 3% on a challenging demand environment.

Yet spending in aggregate is strong. Gartner forecasts worldwide IT spending at $6.31 trillion in 2026, up 13.5%, but it says the growth is led by AI infrastructure and data-centre systems, not services. The broad market backdrop is also firm: FactSet reports blended S&P 500 Q3 earnings growth of 30.2%.

We did not find a sourced view on how interest rates or currencies are moving this group in 2026. Accenture noted a foreign-exchange drag of about 0.8% on Q4 revenue. Our read is that the macro picture is mixed: clients have money, but they are directing it toward AI infrastructure and delaying services decisions.

The addressable market is large. Gartner has IT services as the largest category within a $6.31 trillion total, though the republished table prints the number with a unit error and we could not confirm a growth rate. Pzena puts IT services at roughly 30% of global technology spending.

Demand drivers are cloud migration, modernisation of legacy systems, data readiness and AI deployment. Infosys said AI services reached 10.5% of revenue and grew 29% sequentially. Cognizant's CEO said over 50% of code at the company is AI-assisted.

The secular question is whether AI makes the same work cheaper and therefore smaller. ICICI Securities projects the share of global technology spending going to IT services falling by 8 percentage points over calendar 2023 to 2026, based on Gartner data, and 20% to 40% productivity gains in coding, testing and support. Consulting is cyclical and can be cut quickly, while managed services contracts run longer.
Our read is that the market will still grow, but at lower rates than the 2021 peak, and that AI will redistribute revenue among vendors.

Porter's five forces point to moderate profitability. Rivalry is intense, since firms compete on price and talent, and clients rebid contracts. Accenture says pricing was lower in many areas in Q4 and that clients retain it on a non-exclusive basis. Buyer power is high, with renewal price step-downs up to roughly 6% to 7% from 3% to 4%.

Supplier power sits with employees and technology partners, because skilled engineers and platform access are scarce. The threat of new entrants is mixed: low for small boutiques, high for AI-native firms that sell outcomes rather than hours, which Accenture lists among competitors. The threat of substitutes comes from in-house teams, global capability centres and software with embedded AI.

Concentration is low at the whole-industry level but leaders are large: Accenture's fiscal 2026 revenue was $74.2 billion, Cognizant guides to about $22.1 billion, and EPAM's Q3 revenue was $1.43 billion. We did not find a sourced market-share table.

Moats come from scale, client history and industry platforms. Accenture says 85% of its top 200 commercial clients have partnered with it for 20 years or more, and Cognizant's TriZetto platform processes roughly two-thirds of US healthcare claims, per Pzena.

Politically, the key exposures are immigration and trade. Accenture's 10-K flags rising costs of H-1B and similar visas and the threat or imposition of tariffs and trade restrictions. Cognizant said policy uncertainty delayed client decisions. We found no new statute this quarter that directly changes sub-industry economics.

Technologically, AI is both product and threat. Accenture states that work performed by its people has been and will continue to be replaced by automation, which has led and may lead to reduced demand. The sector sold off in February after Anthropic launched plug-ins for its Claude Cowork agent and Palantir said it compresses SAP migration timelines from years to weeks, per Business Today.

Companies are positioning as AI enablers. Accenture and Anthropic each committed at least $1 billion over five years to a partnership, and Accenture announced three cybersecurity deals worth $4.18 billion in June. EPAM launched Frontier AI Services.

Social and legal pressures include data privacy, AI governance and workforce impacts. Pzena notes clients are pressing vendors to share AI savings and moving to fixed-price and outcome-based contracts. Environmental factors are minor for this asset-light group. We did not find a sourced assessment of specific AI regulation costs.

Revenue growth is low single digit at most leaders, while margins have held. Accenture's adjusted operating margin rose 20 basis points to 15.8% in fiscal 2026, Cognizant's adjusted margin rose 30 basis points to 16.3% in Q3, and EPAM's non-GAAP margin rose to 16.7% from 16.0%. Infosys guides 20% to 22%.

Damodaran's January 2026 US Computer Services group (64 firms) shows a gross margin of 24.3%, net margin of 4.5% and pre-tax operating margin of 7.4%. The gap with the leaders reflects the group's many smaller firms, in our view. Damodaran's normalised ROIC is 37.4%, although the page's own dating is inconsistent.

Operating leverage is moderate: costs are mostly salaries and can be flexed through hiring, but cutting staff takes time. Revenue per employee at Accenture is about $90,000. Cash generation is strong: Accenture's free cash flow was $11.6 billion in FY26, about 16% of revenue, and Cognizant's Q3 free cash flow was $925 million. Cognizant's year-to-date free cash flow is lower than a year earlier ($1.58 billion versus $1.88 billion).

Capital intensity is low, so cash goes to buybacks, dividends and acquisitions. Accenture returned $11.5 billion in fiscal 2026; EPAM plans a $500 million accelerated share repurchase and commits to returning at least 50% of free cash flow from 2027 to 2029.

Guidance, not consensus, is the best evidence we have. Accenture guides fiscal 2027 revenue growth of 3% to 6% in local currency and GAAP EPS of $14.39 to $14.81, up 6% to 9%. The midpoint of the revenue range is above the analyst average of 3.9% (LSEG), per Reuters coverage.

Cognizant guides 2026 adjusted EPS of $5.72 to $5.79, up 8% to 10%, and a Q4 revenue range of $5.49 billion to $5.57 billion. EPAM guides 2026 non-GAAP EPS of $13.23 to $13.31 and Q4 revenue of $1.405 billion to $1.420 billion, which is minus 0.2% to plus 0.9% year on year. Infosys's FY27 guide is 1% to 2%.

Estimate revisions: Infosys cut its guide, but Accenture's guide proved conservative at Accenture, where Q4 revenue of $18.68 billion beat its own $17.75 billion to $18.40 billion guide. We could not obtain sub-industry consensus EPS growth or revision data, and FactSet's sector figures are for the wider S&P 500.

Our view: low-single-digit revenue growth combined with buybacks supports mid-to-high single-digit EPS growth, as Accenture's adjusted EPS grew 8% in FY26. The risk to that view is renewal price cuts arriving faster than new AI work, which is not visible yet in margins.

The group is cheap against its own history. At 30 June 2026, Pzena measured Accenture at 8.7x forward earnings versus a five-year median of 24.3x, Cognizant at 6.7x versus 15.2x, and Globant at 4.6x versus 29.6x. Those readings predate the October rebound, when Accenture jumped about 22% in a day and Cognizant about 8%, so current multiples are higher; we did not find a current sub-industry forward P/E.

Damodaran's January 2026 US Computer Services group trades at 14.1x EV/EBITDA and 19.3x EV/EBIT. The S&P 500 trades at 18.7x forward earnings, below its five-year average of 19.8x and ten-year average of 19.1x.

Free cash flow yields are high. Pzena reports double-digit FCF yields for Accenture, Cognizant and Globant at June 30, and about 12% of Accenture's market cap returned annually through dividends and buybacks. Accenture's FY26 free cash flow of $11.6 billion is the cash flow underneath that yield.

Our read is that the price implied low or negative long-term growth in June. The October guidance reduced that gap but did not close it. Pzena argues the stocks are priced for a difficult transition with little credit for a central role in enterprise AI adoption; investors who disagree point to price step-downs and slowing guidance at Cognizant and Infosys.

Momentum has been poor, with a sharp reversal. Accenture fell 17.97% on 18 June to $127.98, a drop of 24.8% in a week, after cutting its FY26 growth forecast; Infosys, Cognizant and IBM fell 5.7% to 10.5% and Capgemini 8.9%. Before the 1 October rally, Accenture was down about a third in 2026.

On 1 October Accenture rose about 22%, its best day on record, Cognizant about 8% and IBM about 3%, while US-listed Wipro and Infosys gained 6% to 7%. An interviewee noted that many institutions feel underinvested in software, so part of the move may be rotation.

Indian IT shares were hit in parallel. Business Today recorded sharp falls at Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCL Tech and Tech Mahindra in February. We did not obtain a current Nifty IT year-to-date figure, and ETF flow, short interest and breadth data for this sub-industry were not publicly available to us.
Our read is that positioning is now less one-sided than in June, but the stocks remain driven by the AI-disruption narrative rather than quarterly earnings, which have been steady.

Internet Services & Infrastructure is a small, mixed group whose companies sell the plumbing of the web, and the AI buildout is splitting it. Cloudflare grew revenue 39% to $782.5 million and DigitalOcean 40% to $321 million, while Akamai grew 6% with profit margins falling and GoDaddy grew 6%. Verisign remains a 67%-margin toll road on .com. Cloud infrastructure spending hit $167.7 billion in the September quarter, up 55%. We found no sub-industry consensus or multiples; sector-level data show Information Technology at 17.3x forward earnings, its lowest since March 2020.

These companies run pieces of the internet's plumbing and rent them to other businesses. Some deliver and protect web traffic (Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly), some register and host domains and websites (GoDaddy, Verisign), and some rent simple cloud servers to developers (DigitalOcean). Revenue is mostly subscriptions or usage fees. The giant cloud providers (Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet) are classified elsewhere in GICS, as are IT consulting firms in the neighbouring sub-industry. Snowflake-style data platforms and software-heavy security vendors are, we believe, not here either, but we could not verify GICS constituent lists.

Content delivery and edge networks: Servers placed around the world that store and serve websites, video and software downloads close to the user, so pages load faster and the origin site carries less load. e.g. Akamai delivery, Fastly, Cloudflare CDN

Security and traffic protection: Services that sit in front of a customer's site or network to block attacks, bots and fraud, and to control who gets in. Sold as subscriptions, often bundled. e.g. Akamai Security, Cloudflare Zero Trust and DDoS protection, Fastly Security

Cloud servers and AI compute for developers: Rented virtual machines, storage and, increasingly, graphics chips (GPUs) for running AI models, aimed at developers and small and mid-sized firms rather than large enterprises. e.g. DigitalOcean Droplets and Inference Engine, Akamai Cloud Infrastructure Services

Domain registration and registry: A registry runs the master database of a domain ending such as .com; a registrar sells names to the public. Registries charge a regulated fee per name per year. e.g. Verisign (.com, .net registry), GoDaddy (registrar)
Web hosting and small-business tools: Packages that give a small business a website, email, online store and marketing tools for a monthly fee. e.g. GoDaddy hosting, website builder, Airo AI tools
Developer and edge platforms: Services that let programmers run code at the network edge, close to users, instead of in a central data center. e.g. Cloudflare Workers, Fastly Compute

Internet traffic, bots and attacks: More traffic and more attacks mean more spend on delivery and security. Security is now the larger and faster-growing line at Akamai and Fastly, while delivery is shrinking at Akamai.

AI workloads: AI model training and inference need compute, networking and security. This is lifting DigitalOcean, Cloudflare and Akamai's cloud unit, but it also pulls down gross margins because chips and capacity cost money up front.

Pricing power and contract terms: Verisign's .com price can rise up to 7% in each of four years of a six-year cycle, which flows almost entirely to profit. Others compete on price and bundle products.
Small-business formation and web habits: GoDaddy's customer count and revenue per customer follow small-business creation and how people build online presences, increasingly through AI tools.

Capital intensity: Cloud growth requires servers and chips ahead of revenue. Akamai's capital spending rose to about $1.02 billion in nine months from about $615 million, which trims free cash flow before the revenue arrives.

Customer concentration in new AI deals: Large multi-year AI contracts can add a lot of revenue quickly but make results depend on a few customers, as Fastly's top ten customers now being 39% of revenue shows.
CDN (content delivery network): A network of servers that copies content close to users. The original business of Akamai and Fastly; it is now a slower-growing, price-competitive product.
Registry vs. registrar: A registry (Verisign for .com) operates a domain ending and earns a set fee per name. A registrar (GoDaddy) sells names to customers and competes on price and service.
Domain name base: The number of registered names in a registry. Verisign's revenue grows with this base and with price increases, so analysts track net adds each quarter.
Renewal rate: The share of expiring domains that are renewed. High renewal rates are what make registry revenue so predictable.
ARR (annual recurring revenue): The current quarter's recurring revenue annualized. Used by DigitalOcean and others as a gauge of momentum before revenue shows it.
RPO (remaining performance obligations): Contracted revenue not yet recognized. Rising RPO signals bookings that will turn into revenue, and matters for companies signing multi-year deals.
Net retention: Revenue from existing customers this year divided by the same customers' revenue last year. Above 100% means customers are spending more over time.
DDoS: Distributed denial of service: an attack that floods a site with traffic to knock it offline. Defending against it is a core security product.
Edge: Computing and caching done in many locations near users rather than in a few central data centers. Reduces delay.
Inference: Running a trained AI model to answer a request. It is repetitive, latency-sensitive work that edge and developer clouds hope to win.
Neocloud: A newer cloud provider built around AI chips (CoreWeave, Nebius, Crusoe). A competitor to developer clouds and a sign of how fast AI compute demand is growing.

Normalized EBITDA / non-GAAP margin: Company-defined profit measures that exclude stock compensation and one-offs. Useful for comparison, but they flatter companies with large stock pay, so check the GAAP figure too.
Whether Akamai's cloud infrastructure services build, backed by more than $14 billion of multi-year commitments and 2027 growth guidance of 17% to 22%, arrives on schedule while margins fall.
Cloudflare's gross margin, which fell about three points year over year to 72.4% in the quarter.
Verisign's .com wholesale price: contract terms allow up to 7% increases in the final four years of the pricing period, and commentators read 2026 as the first year an increase is possible.
GoDaddy's ability to turn AI tools (Airo above $100 million of annualized bookings) into growth faster than AI website generators erode its basics.
The AI capex cycle: Amazon alone expects about $220 billion of 2026 capital spending, and its trailing free cash flow turned negative.
Cloudflare, Akamai Technologies, GoDaddy, Verisign, DigitalOcean, Fastly

Subscriptions and usage fees dominate. Akamai reports Security ($622 million in Q3 2026), Delivery and other ($391 million) and Cloud Infrastructure Services ($109 million); GoDaddy sells domains, hosting and commerce tools, and Verisign earns almost all revenue from per-name fees on .com and .net. Cloudflare and Fastly sell network and security subscriptions plus usage.

Customers range from consumers and small businesses (GoDaddy has 20.5 million customers) to large enterprises and media firms (Akamai, Fastly) and developers (Cloudflare, DigitalOcean). Verisign's direct customers are registrars, who pay it per domain per year.

The main costs are network capacity and data-center space, depreciation of servers and chips, bandwidth, and staff. Cloudflare's non-GAAP gross margin fell to 72.4% from 75.3% in Q3 2026, showing how infrastructure cost bites. Verisign's cost base is tiny, with 928 employees.

Pricing power is highest for Verisign, whose .com price can rise up to 7% in each of the last four years of a six-year period under its agreements. For delivery it is low: Akamai's Delivery revenue fell 3%. Security, bundled and sticky, supports better pricing.

Assets are networks of servers, fiber and data centers, intangible assets (domains, customer bases) and cash. Liabilities include convertible debt: Akamai had $7.57 billion of convertible notes at 30 Sep 2026, GoDaddy $2.69 billion of net debt, Verisign $1.79 billion of senior notes.

Mixed. Verisign is asset-light (nine-month capex of $33.6 million). Network and cloud businesses are more capital-intensive, and AI demand is raising that: Akamai spent about $1.02 billion on capex in nine months against about $615 million a year earlier.

No official size exists for this sub-industry, and we did not find a source that totals it. The related market is large: Synergy puts global cloud infrastructure services spending at $167.7 billion in Q3 2026, up 55%, with $558 billion over twelve months. Most of that goes to the hyperscalers, not this sub-industry.

Main segments are content delivery and security, developer and AI clouds, domain registries and registrars, and hosting and small-business web tools. Revenue mixes differ widely: Akamai's Security was $622 million against $109 million for Cloud Infrastructure Services in Q3 2026.

The group sits between hyperscale cloud and the end customer. Suppliers are chip makers, data-center landlords and carriers; customers are businesses that need their sites fast and safe. Hyperscalers are both suppliers and rivals: Amazon, Microsoft and Google hold 61% of cloud infrastructure spending between them.

It evolved from hosting and CDN to security and edge computing, and now to AI. Akamai has pivoted toward cloud infrastructure, targeting $1.1 billion to $1.3 billion of that revenue in 2027. Cloudflare calls itself the development platform for the AI-powered Internet.

The industry is US-centred: the United States is 44% of global cloud spending. Akamai's revenue split is $559 million US and $563 million international in Q3 2026. GoDaddy and Verisign are US companies selling globally; the .com space has about 182.5 million names.

There are few large listed pure plays: Cloudflare, Akamai, GoDaddy, Verisign, DigitalOcean and Fastly are the main names we found. We could not verify an official constituent list. Against hyperscalers and neoclouds, the real competitor set is far bigger.

Leaders differ by niche. Verisign is the sole .com registry operator through 30 Nov 2030. GoDaddy manages about 81 million of roughly 387 million registered domains (about 21%). In cloud infrastructure, Amazon holds 26%, Microsoft 19% and Google 16%. We did not find CDN or security share data.

It is a mix. Domain registries are concentrated by contract; registrars, CDNs and developer clouds are contested. Verisign names GoDaddy, Google, Identity Digital, Nominet, PIR and Radix as registry rivals for domain demand.

Barriers vary. A registry needs an ICANN agreement; a CDN needs global network scale and years of traffic data. Neoclouds show chip access, not tradition, can be an entry ticket: Synergy counts nine neoclouds in the top 40 cloud providers.

Economies of scale are strong in network and security: more traffic improves threat detection and spreads fixed cost. Akamai's operating cash flow was 39% of revenue in Q3 2026, while the scale advantage of hyperscalers is visible in AWS's roughly 39% operating margin on $46 billion of revenue.

Delivery is increasingly commoditized and priced down (Akamai's Delivery fell 3%). Security, edge platforms and registry are more differentiated, and AI inference could go either way. Domain registration is a regulated commodity at wholesale level.

Customers hold the power in delivery and hosting, where switching is easy and big customers negotiate; Fastly's top ten customers were 39% of revenue. Suppliers (chip and memory vendors, data-center owners) gain power when AI demand is tight; Akamai is buying capacity ahead of demand.

Revenue follows internet traffic, security spending and AI compute demand. Cloud infrastructure spending grew 55% in Q3 2026, with AI services about a third of the market. Domain revenue follows the name base (+6.1% y/y) and price.

Margins depend on mix and utilization. Security is more profitable than delivery; Verisign runs near a 67% operating margin on its fee model. New AI capacity weighs on margins first: Akamai's non-GAAP operating margin fell 6 points to 25%.

Key costs: bandwidth and transit, server and GPU hardware, power and space, and stock compensation. Akamai's nine-month capex rose from about $615 million to $1.02 billion, and Cloudflare's gross margin slipped 2.9 points.

Rate sensitivity is moderate. Several firms carry zero-coupon converts (Cloudflare's 2030 notes are $2.0 billion at 0%), which keeps interest cost low, and Verisign and GoDaddy borrow at fixed rates. The bigger rate effect is on valuation of long-duration growth names such as Cloudflare, at about 190x forward earnings.

Inflation matters through pricing and component costs. Verisign's contract allows up to 7% annual price increases in four of six years, which offsets inflation. Unemployment and GDP matter through small-business formation (GoDaddy) and advertising and e-commerce traffic. We did not find a published sensitivity estimate.

Mixed: secular growth in security, edge and AI compute, defensive characteristics in domain registries (75.2% renewal rate), and cyclical exposure in small-business and media-linked delivery. Akamai's guidance for faster growth in 2027 rests on the AI-driven cloud build.

Wide dispersion. Q3 2026 revenue growth: Cloudflare +39%, DigitalOcean +40%, Fastly +20%, GoDaddy +6%, Akamai +6%, Verisign +5.7%. Damodaran's 29-firm Software (Internet) group, a rough proxy and not the GICS sub-industry, had a net margin of -0.93%.

Margins diverge. Verisign's operating margin is about 66.9% on our calculation from its release; Akamai's non-GAAP operating margin is 25%; Cloudflare's 17.5%; Fastly's non-GAAP gross margin is 65.8%. Damodaran's Software (Internet) group shows 62.6% gross and 18.6% operating margin (pre-stock-pay).

We did not find published industry ROE or ROIC for this exact group, and we do not estimate them. Single-name: Verisign's low capital need and 67% margin imply very high returns on capital, though its negative equity base makes ROE hard to interpret (our judgment; equity figures not collected).

Leverage is common but manageable. Akamai has $7.57 billion of convertible notes against $4.24 billion of cash and securities; GoDaddy has $3.81 billion of debt and $1.12 billion cash; Verisign has $1.79 billion of notes and $476 million of cash; DigitalOcean has about $462 million of debt plus about $924 million of leases.

Free cash flow is strong. GoDaddy generated $480.8 million in Q3 and targets about $1.8 billion for 2026. DigitalOcean's adjusted FCF margin was 41%. Cloudflare's was 10% ($82.1 million). Fastly produced $25.2 million in Q3 (about 13% of revenue by our calculation).

Capex needs are rising where AI is involved. Akamai's nine-month capex was about $1.02 billion; Cloudflare's Q1 2026 property purchases were only $65.2 million; Verisign's nine-month capex was $33.6 million.

Valuations span extremes. Damodaran's January 2026 data show 30.3x EV/EBITDA for Software (Internet) (positive-EBITDA firms) and 11.5x for Information Services, versus 19.7x for the whole US market. Cloudflare traded near 190x forward earnings at 30 Oct 2026. We did not find a verified multiple for the other names.

Regulation: Verisign's .com price and terms are bound by agreements with ICANN and the US Department of Commerce, and ICANN policy changes could add costs. Privacy rules (GDPR, NIS 2) raise compliance costs, and China requires gTLD licenses. Antitrust and content-liability debates also touch CDNs and security.

AI cuts both ways. It drives demand for compute, security and bot management, but GoDaddy says AI website generators and closed AI ecosystems could reduce demand for its website products. Verisign warns AI and social platforms may lower demand for domain names.
Demographics barely matter. The relevant population is businesses and developers, not age groups. Small-business formation affects GoDaddy, and we did not find a source that ties it to demographics.

Behavior is shifting: people reach information through AI assistants rather than websites, and businesses build in platforms rather than on their own domains. This is a risk to domains, hosting and traffic-based delivery, which is the thesis behind Verisign's and GoDaddy's AI risk language.

New competitors are plentiful: neoclouds such as CoreWeave, Nebius and Crusoe grow quickly, and Synergy now ranks nine in the top 40 providers. Hyperscalers take 61% of cloud spend and are growing faster than the smaller providers.

Geopolitical and supply risks: dependence on chips, memory and power for AI capacity, and cross-border regulation. Akamai said it would use note proceeds for accelerated capital expenditure for its cloud build. DNS operators like Verisign face state-level cyber threats.

Substitutes: hyperscaler CDNs and security, in-house infrastructure, and non-domain identities such as social profiles and app stores. Delivery shrinking at Akamai (-3%) shows the substitution is already real for the oldest product.
AI inference and agent traffic could make edge networks and developer clouds a growth channel: DigitalOcean guides to 2027 revenue growth of 60% or more and Akamai to 17% to 22%.
Security keeps growing faster than delivery: Akamai Security +9% and Fastly Security +32% in Q3 2026.
Verisign's pricing and base growth (6.1% in Q3) give a steady, high-margin income stream, with the new .web domain on track.
AI-assisted tools could raise revenue per customer at GoDaddy: Airo passed $100 million of annualized bookings.
Hyperscalers and neoclouds capture most AI cloud spending, and the group's capital-intensive entrants risk lower returns on new builds.
AI search, agents and website generators could reduce demand for domains and traditional hosting.
Delivery commoditization continues to erode the oldest revenue pool (Akamai Delivery -3%).
Gross and operating margins are falling at companies investing early in AI (Cloudflare, Akamai).

We think the group will keep splitting into three types over the next three to five years. Registry-style franchises (Verisign) should keep compounding slowly with pricing and name growth, with AI-driven demand for domains as the main unknown. Security and edge platforms (Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly) are priced and guided for acceleration, but depend on turning AI traffic into revenue without losing margin. Small-business web platforms (GoDaddy) are fighting for relevance as AI changes how sites are made. The Q3 2026 guidance from Akamai (2028 revenue above $7.0 billion) and DigitalOcean (60% growth in 2027) shows how much the market is leaning on AI, so a slowdown in AI spending would hit the faster-growing names hardest.

This group is a levered play on technology spending rather than on the broad economy. FactSet shows S&P 500 earnings growth for Q3 2026 running at 31.4% blended, with the Information Technology sector at 69.2%, so the backdrop for tech buyers is strong. Those are sector-level numbers, not this sub-industry; no sub-industry aggregate was available to us.

The cycle is being set by AI infrastructure rather than rates. Amazon alone expects about $220 billion of capital spending in 2026, and its trailing free cash flow has turned negative. Cloud spending grew 55% in Q3. That demand spills over into the smaller infrastructure names, but also pushes up their costs.

On rates and inflation, we did not collect a current policy path. The group's exposure is indirect: zero-coupon converts (Cloudflare's 2030 notes are at 0%) limit interest cost, and Verisign's contractual price increases of up to 7% a year are a built-in hedge against inflation. Currency matters mostly for Akamai, where revenue grew 6% reported and 7% in constant currency.

The addressable market is hard to size for this exact sub-industry. The adjacent cloud infrastructure market reached $167.7 billion in Q3 2026, up 55% from a year earlier, with $558 billion over twelve months and AI services about a third of the total. Earlier, Synergy had Q2 at $143 billion, up 43%, with generative AI services growing 165%.

This group captures only a small fraction of that. The structural drivers are more traffic, more attacks, AI inference and agent traffic, and more small businesses online. Akamai targets $1.1 billion to $1.3 billion of cloud infrastructure revenue in 2027 and cites more than $14 billion of multi-year commitments signed this year. DigitalOcean's AI-customer ARR rose to $376 million.

Demand is mixed in cyclicality. Domain registrations are stable and recurring: Verisign's base reached 182.5 million names, up 6.1%, with a 75.2% renewal rate. Delivery is mature: Akamai's Delivery revenue fell 3%. Demographics matter little, and we did not find a long-term forecast for the group specifically.

Porter's five forces show a split picture. Rivalry is intense in delivery and developer cloud, mild in registries. Threat of new entrants is high in AI compute, where neoclouds rank nine of the top 40 providers, but low in .com, where Verisign is the sole operator through 30 Nov 2030.

Buyer power is high for large customers: Fastly's top ten customers were 39% of revenue. Supplier power sits with chip, memory and data-center providers, especially while AI demand is tight; Akamai is raising capex to secure capacity. Threat of substitutes comes from hyperscaler services and AI tools: GoDaddy flags AI website tools and closed ecosystems as a risk.

Shares are known only in adjacent markets: Amazon 26%, Microsoft 19% and Google 16% of cloud infrastructure spending in Q3 2026. GoDaddy manages about 21% of registered domains. Moats are strongest at Verisign (contractual), then security and edge platforms with network scale, and weakest in generic hosting.

Regulation is concentrated on the domain business. Verisign operates under the .com Registry Agreement with ICANN, renewed in November 2024, and a Cooperative Agreement with the Department of Commerce; price rises are capped at 7% in each of the final four years of a six-year period. Commentators noted that the contract language allowed an increase from late October 2026, potentially from $10.26 to $10.97. We did not independently confirm the announced effective date.

Other political and legal factors include GDPR and NIS 2 compliance costs and China's license requirements. Technologically, AI is the disruptor: it creates inference and bot-management demand at Cloudflare, DigitalOcean and Akamai, and creates substitution risk for GoDaddy and domains.

Emerging risks include AI-enabled cyberattacks on DNS and networks, and restructuring around AI: Cloudflare disclosed a workforce reduction and restructuring charges as it moves to an agentic AI-first operating model.

Economics vary sharply by model. Verisign earns about a 67% operating margin on $443 million of quarterly revenue (our calculation) and spent only $33.6 million on capex in nine months. GoDaddy's normalized EBITDA margin was 33.5% with free cash flow of $480.8 million in Q3. DigitalOcean's adjusted EBITDA margin was 45% and adjusted FCF margin 41%.

The infrastructure-heavy names show operating leverage under pressure. Cloudflare's non-GAAP operating margin was 17.5% and its GAAP operating margin -8.7%, with FCF at 10% of revenue. Akamai's non-GAAP operating margin dropped 6 points to 25% while operating cash flow stayed at 39% of revenue. Fastly's GAAP operating loss narrowed to 5.9% of revenue from 18.2%.

Damodaran's January 2026 data, which are US-wide and not a GICS match, show Software (Internet) at 62.6% gross margin and 18.6% operating margin (before stock pay) and Information Services at 34.1% gross and 13.5% operating margin, against 14.4% for all US firms. We did not find industry ROE or ROIC figures for this group.

Third-quarter reports were mostly strong at the top line. Cloudflare raised full-year revenue guidance to $2.963 to $2.964 billion and Q4 to $845 to $846 million. DigitalOcean guided to 2026 revenue of $1.208 to $1.211 billion and 2027 growth of 60% or more. Fastly guided 2026 to $744 to $748 million.

Akamai is the swing case: it guided 2026 revenue to $4.44 to $4.465 billion with a 25% non-GAAP operating margin, 2027 growth of 17% to 22% in constant currency, and 2028 revenue above $7.0 billion. That implies a sharp acceleration from 6% now and rests on AI cloud commitments. GoDaddy expects revenue toward the high end of $5.215 to $5.255 billion. We did not capture Verisign's current-year guidance from the release text we opened, so we leave it out.

We did not find consensus estimates or revisions for the sub-industry. At sector level, FactSet shows the Information Technology blended Q3 growth rate rising to 69.2% on positive surprises, but that is dominated by other sub-industries. Our read is that the guidance for Akamai and DigitalOcean is the part most likely to be disputed, because it assumes AI demand holds.

The group has no single multiple. At the sector level, FactSet puts Information Technology at 17.3x forward earnings on 5 Nov 2026, below its 25-year average of 20.0x and the lowest since March 2020; the S&P 500 is at 17.7x against a 10-year average of 19.1x. This is a different set of companies, and the sector has been dominated by hardware and semiconductors.

Within the group, valuation gaps are extreme. Cloudflare was near 190x forward earnings at the 30 Oct 2026 close, against an average of about 173x since mid-2023, and its share price was up about 35% in 2026 through 2 November (before its Q3 results). Damodaran's January 2026 data show Software (Internet) at 30.3x EV/EBITDA for firms with positive EBITDA and Information Services at 11.5x.

We could not obtain verified current multiples for Akamai, GoDaddy, Verisign or DigitalOcean, so we do not quote them. In our judgment, Cloudflare is priced for sustained growth near 40%, while the slower names (Akamai, GoDaddy) must show that AI-driven acceleration is real before the market pays for it.
We did not find sub-industry ETF flow, short-interest or institutional-positioning data for this group, and we do not estimate them.

Price momentum is visible only for Cloudflare, which was up about 35% year to date at $265 on 2 November but about 28% below its 6 October high of $370, before its Q3 results. Fastly and Akamai share moves after results were reported in news items we did not open, so we leave them out.

At the broad level, FactSet's data show the S&P 500 forward P/E fell from 22.0 at the end of 2025 to 17.7 because estimates rose 33.6% while the index rose 7.4%. The setup for the group is therefore one of rising earnings expectations and falling sector multiples, but with this sub-industry's results depending heavily on a handful of AI-linked names.

Electronic Equipment & Instruments is in a strong earnings phase, led by test and measurement and machine vision. Keysight's July-quarter revenue rose about 36% and orders 56% on AI and communications demand, Teledyne raised its full-year outlook, and Cognex posted a 32.2% operating margin. Weak spots are memory-cost pressure on Zebra's gross margin, slower Trimble recurring-revenue growth and flat Itron utility hardware. US manufacturing is expanding, with the ISM index at 55.5 in October. Sub-industry forward multiples and consensus were not available to us; the technology sector trades at 17.3x, a multi-year low.

These companies make the instruments, sensors and electronic systems that other businesses use to measure, test, locate, scan and control things. Customers are engineers, factories, utilities, governments, defence agencies and logistics firms, not consumers. Revenue comes from hardware, increasingly with software and recurring subscriptions attached. GICS also puts here scanners, machine vision, GPS positioning and smart meters. Passive parts, connectors and display makers sit in the neighbouring Electronic Components sub-industry, and contract assemblers sit in Electronic Manufacturing Services.
Test and measurement: Oscilloscopes, signal analysers and network testers that engineers use to design and verify chips, radios, cars and data-centre links. e.g. Keysight, Teledyne LeCroy
Machine vision and barcode scanning: Cameras and software that read codes and inspect parts on production lines and in warehouses. e.g. Cognex vision systems, Zebra scanners and mobile computers
Positioning and field technology: GPS and laser positioning hardware paired with software for surveying, construction, farming and trucking. e.g. Trimble
Smart meters and grid devices: Electricity, gas and water meters with communications and software that let utilities read and manage networks remotely. e.g. Itron
Imaging and sensors: Thermal, X-ray and other sensors and cameras for industrial, scientific and defence customers. e.g. Teledyne FLIR and Teledyne Digital Imaging
Fuelling and vehicle technology: Pumps, payment terminals, tank monitoring and diagnostics sold to fuel retailers and vehicle repair shops. e.g. Vontier (Gilbarco Veeder-Root, Matco)

Customer R&D and capital spending: Test and measurement follows engineering budgets in 5G/6G, AI data centres, semiconductors, aerospace and automotive. When customers launch new technology generations, orders for new instruments jump.
Industrial and logistics activity: Scanners, vision systems and positioning gear sell into factories, warehouses and construction. Weak manufacturing or freight slows orders within a few quarters.
Defence and government budgets: Imaging, sensing and electronics makers with defence exposure carry multi-year contracts, which smooths revenue but ties it to appropriations.
Utility capital plans: Meter makers depend on regulated utilities approving grid upgrades. Orders arrive in large rollouts, so revenue is lumpy but backlog is visible.
Component costs and tariffs: Memory, chips and import duties change the bill of materials. Makers either pass costs on in price or accept lower gross margin.
Software and recurring mix: A higher share of subscriptions and services raises margins and cuts cyclicality, which is why portfolio changes often target software.
Acquisitions: Roll-up buyers add products and distribution, lifting reported growth and, after integration costs, margins. Most large names here are serial acquirers.
Book-to-bill: Orders received divided by revenue shipped in a period. Above 1 means the order book is growing, which points to future revenue.
Backlog: Orders booked but not yet delivered or recognized. It gives visibility, especially for defence and utility projects.
ARR (annual recurring revenue): The yearly value of subscriptions and software contracts that repeat. Investors pay more for it because it is steadier than hardware sales.
Organic growth: Growth excluding acquisitions, disposals and currency. It shows whether the existing business is expanding.
Core sales: Vontier's version of organic growth, excluding acquired and divested businesses and currency effects.
Installed base: The equipment already in customers' hands. It generates calibration, service, software and upgrade revenue.
Calibration and service: Recurring work to keep instruments accurate and repaired. It is steady, higher-margin revenue behind one-off equipment sales.
Capex cycle: Customers' spending on new equipment. Instrument orders typically rise and fall with it, ahead of or alongside the economy.
Bill of materials (BOM): The cost of components in a device. Memory chips are an increasing share, so chip price moves feed straight into gross margins.
Non-GAAP operating margin: Operating profit excluding items such as acquisition amortization and restructuring. It is the figure most of these companies guide to, so check the reconciliation.
Machine vision: Cameras plus software that let machines see, used to inspect products and guide robots. Demand follows factory automation and logistics volumes.
AMI (advanced metering infrastructure): Meters that report usage by network rather than being read by hand. Utilities buy them in multi-year rollouts.
Keysight reports fiscal Q4 on 19 Nov against guidance of $1.93-1.95B revenue, and says demand is strong but supply availability limits conversion of orders.
Whether memory costs keep squeezing hardware makers: Zebra's gross margin fell 2.3 points on memory and mix, and contract DRAM prices are still rising though more slowly.
Trimble's ARR growth of 11% is its key recurring-revenue measure, and its Q3 release updates full-year guidance without explaining the change.
Utility and scientific-instrument budgets: Itron's bookings rose 27% to $482M, while an ISM respondent says global demand for capital scientific instruments has slowed.
Rates and tariffs: the Fed held at 3.75-4.00% with two dissents favoring a hike, and Keysight is still processing IEEPA tariff refunds.
Keysight Technologies, Teledyne Technologies, Trimble, Zebra Technologies, Cognex, Itron, Vontier

Revenue comes mainly from selling instruments and devices, then software, subscriptions, calibration and repair. Keysight sells test equipment and software to about 40,000 customers a year. Trimble counts ARR of $2.56B and Itron reports ARR of $423M, up 25%, showing how recurring revenue is growing alongside hardware.

Customers are engineers and operators rather than consumers: communications and chip designers, aerospace and defence, automakers, factories, logistics operators, utilities and fuel retailers. Orders come from budgeted projects, which makes revenue lumpy but visible in backlog; Teledyne cites funded backlog of nearly $5.3B.

Principal costs are components and manufacturing, research and development, and selling. Keysight spent $1,007M on R&D in fiscal 2025, roughly 19% of revenue on our arithmetic from its $5.4B of revenue. Damodaran's broad Electronics (General) group shows R&D of 4.23% of sales, so the leaders spend far more on engineering than the average group member.

Pricing power depends on measurement accuracy, the installed base and software lock-in. Cognex's gross margin of 70.8% and Keysight's segment margins of 31-34% show how much differentiated products earn, while Zebra's 45.7% gross margin fell on memory costs it could only partly pass on.

Main assets are intellectual property, acquired goodwill and intangibles, and inventory and receivables. Keysight booked $712M of goodwill on its Spirent purchase. Liabilities are modest: Keysight has net cash of roughly $88M on our arithmetic from its balance sheet and Cognex holds $846M with no debt, though Vontier carries net debt of $1,647M.

The group is asset-light compared with semiconductors. Teledyne spent $33M on capex against $352.5M of operating cash flow in Q3, and Zebra spent $50M against $711M over nine months. Design and engineering are the real investment; assembly is largely outsourced or modest in scale.

No authoritative market-size figure was available to us. Published test-and-measurement estimates differ widely by scope, and the sources we could open did not give one. We therefore size the group by its leaders: Keysight revenue was $5.4B in fiscal 2025, Teledyne $1.68B in one quarter, Zebra $1.61B in a quarter.

Main segments are communications and electronic test (Keysight CSG revenue $1,345M, EISG $501M in the July quarter), imaging and sensing (Teledyne Digital Imaging $903M), enterprise mobility and data capture (Zebra), software-enabled positioning (Trimble), vision (Cognex) and grid and fuelling equipment (Itron, Vontier).

In the value chain these firms buy chips, memory, optics and sensors from component suppliers, and sell to engineers, operators and system integrators. Zebra says rising memory component costs squeezed its gross margin, which shows how exposed they are to the electronic-component tier upstream.

The industry has shifted from pure hardware to hardware plus software and services, and consolidated through deals. Keysight acquired Spirent for $1,564M and Synopsys's optical solutions group for $580M in October 2025; Teledyne agreed to buy Varex for about $1.1B; Cognex is buying RealSense; Zebra reports organic growth of 11.3% against 22.3% reported growth, the gap being acquisitions and currency.

Geography is global. Keysight's July quarter revenue was 39.5% Americas, 16.6% Europe and 43.9% Asia Pacific. Production relies on Asian supply chains, so trade policy matters; Keysight recorded a $100M receivable for recovered IEEPA tariffs.

There are a few dozen significant competitors, but most niches have only a handful. Keysight says it competes with large firms and with specialised regional players, and sees new entrants and consolidation among customers. Cognex, Zebra and Trimble each face a similarly small set of direct rivals, though we did not find sourced counts.

Leaders by niche: Keysight in electronic and communications test, Teledyne in imaging and instrumentation, Zebra in scanners and mobile computers, Cognex in machine vision, Trimble in positioning and Itron in smart metering. Sourced market shares were unavailable, so we do not quote any. Named rivals such as Rohde & Schwarz or Emerson's NI did not appear in the filings we opened.

The industry is fragmented overall but concentrated within segments, and consolidating through acquisitions. Our read is that scale matters most in test and measurement, where breadth across technologies is a selling point Keysight itself stresses.

Barriers to entry are measurement accuracy, deep engineering know-how, certification, and long relationships with customers who design the instruments into their workflows. High R&D intensity (Keysight about 19% of revenue on our arithmetic) raises the cost of competing at the frontier.

Economies of scale appear in R&D spread over a large installed base, global service networks and purchasing. They show up in margins: Keysight's segments earn 31-34% operating margins against about 10.4% pre-tax operating margin for Damodaran's broad Electronics (General) group.

Products are differentiated at the leading edge and commoditised in simpler categories. Cognex's gross margin of 70.8% reflects differentiation; Zebra's 45.7% and Itron's 40.9% show more hardware-like economics where customers have more choice.

Customers hold bargaining power when buying large utility or retail rollouts, which Itron's multi-year backlog of $4.3B illustrates, but power is weaker for mission-critical instruments with few substitutes. Suppliers, especially memory makers, currently have the upper hand: Zebra cites memory costs and DRAM contract prices keep rising.

Revenue growth follows customer technology spending and industrial activity. Keysight's orders rose 56% in the July quarter, Cognex's logistics and electronics markets posted repeated double-digit quarters, and US manufacturing has expanded for ten months. Government and utility budgets drive the rest.

Operating margins depend on mix (software and recurring revenue versus hardware), volume leverage on fixed R&D, component costs and acquisitions. Cognex lifted operating margin from 20.9% to 32.2% on mix, volume and pricing; Zebra's gross margin fell 2.3 points on memory costs and mix.

Key cost variables are memory and semiconductors, labour for engineering, tariffs, and freight. Contract DRAM prices were still rising in the fourth quarter though gains are narrowing, and the ISM prices index was 75.2, meaning input prices are rising broadly.

Sensitivity to interest rates is moderate. Customers finance capital equipment and acquisitions are debt-funded: Vontier's net leverage is 2.3x, Zebra has $2,578M of debt. The Fed held at 3.75-4.00% on 28 October, said inflation remains elevated, and two members wanted a hike.

Inflation, GDP and unemployment matter through industrial production and capex. The ISM manufacturing index of 55.5 signals expansion, while one ISM respondent says scientific-instrument demand slowed on research-funding and geopolitical uncertainty. Commodity prices matter mainly via components.

The group is cyclical with defensive pockets and secular growth layers. Test equipment and vision are cyclical but supported by AI, communications and automation trends; defence and utility products give some stability through backlog; recurring revenue is a growing stabiliser.

Growth is currently strong and uneven. Keysight revenue grew about 36%, Teledyne 9.4%, Cognex 13%, Trimble 7%, Itron 3%. Vontier fell 2.1% on a disposal but core sales rose 5.7%. Damodaran does not give a growth rate for the broad group.

Margins differ by business. Damodaran's Electronics (General) group, 114 US firms, has a 26.76% gross margin and 10.42% pre-tax operating margin as of January 2026. Leaders are well above: Teledyne 23.9% non-GAAP operating margin, Trimble 27.2%, Vontier 24.3% adjusted, Cognex 32.2%.

Returns on capital are high on Damodaran's data: after-tax ROIC of 24.48% against 10.08% for the total US market, and a ten-year normalized ROIC of 17.47%. The page header says January 2026 but its footer says January 2025, so treat the vintage with caution. Damodaran's ROE column was not on that page, so we do not quote one.

Debt is generally moderate. Keysight has roughly net cash, Cognex has no debt, Itron's net debt is about $737M on our arithmetic from its release, Trimble has $1,533M of debt against $214M of cash and Vontier's net leverage is 2.3x.

Free cash flow conversion is high. Teledyne generated $319.5M of free cash flow in Q3, Cognex $104M, Keysight $403M and Vontier $133M with 107% conversion. Zebra guides to at least $1B for the year. Itron's fell to $96M from $113M.
