There are four revenue models. Originators earn gain on sale, which is volatile. Servicers earn recurring fees: Rocket services a $2.0 trillion book for 9.1 million clients. The GSEs earn net interest and guarantee fees; Fannie's average single-family guarantee fee was 49.1 basis points. Mortgage insurers earn premiums.
Customers are borrowers (direct or through brokers), banks and investors in mortgage bonds. UWM's Q3 volume was about 68% purchase loans. The GSEs' customers are lenders who sell them loans.

Principal costs are compensation, marketing and technology for lenders, funding interest on warehouse and corporate debt, and credit provisions at the GSEs. UWM's Q3 expenses were $576 million, down 10% from Q2. PennyMac said it would cut annualized operating expenses by $160 million by Q1 2027.

Pricing power is limited for originators, because rates are quoted nationwide and brokers shop them. It is stronger for servicers with scale and for the GSEs, which have a duopoly position under federal oversight. Mortgage insurers price in a regulated, competitive market.

Assets are loans held for sale, servicing rights and securities; liabilities are warehouse lines and corporate debt. Rocket's secured and unsecured financing totals about $24.9 billion (our sum of two lines) against $11.4 billion of liquidity. Fannie's net worth is $119.6 billion but it holds a $238 billion senior preferred liquidation preference.

Mostly asset-light operationally but balance-sheet heavy financially. Lenders need little physical capital yet carry large borrowed positions. Fannie Mae's actual available CET1 capital was a deficit of $30 billion at 30 Sep 2026, which shows how thin the GSEs' regulatory capital is against $4.1 trillion of guarantees.

The US residential market is about $2.1 trillion of annual originations in 2026 on the MBA's forecast, shrinking to $1.99 trillion in 2027, around 5 million loans a year against a peak near 14 million. The GSEs guarantee a $4.1 trillion book at Fannie and $3.7 trillion total portfolio at Freddie.

Segments are single-family and multifamily lending, servicing, GSE guarantee and insurance. Fannie's multifamily book is $545 billion and Freddie's $510 billion. Within originations, purchase is $1.42 trillion and refinancing $571 billion in the MBA's 2027 forecast.

The industry sits between homeowners and capital markets. Suppliers are funding banks, bond investors and software vendors; customers are households. It is a link in housing finance between builders and agents upstream and bond buyers downstream.

It evolved from deposit-funded thrifts to non-bank lenders and servicers, and consolidated: Rocket acquired Mr. Cooper, with the combined servicing book now $2.0 trillion. GICS merged the old thrifts group into this sub-industry in 2023.

Activity is overwhelmingly US-centered, since the GSEs and these lenders operate domestically. GICS also includes building societies and similar institutions abroad, but the large listed names in this brief are American.
There are a few large players and many small ones. Rocket, UWM and PennyMac are the largest listed non-bank lenders; Fannie and Freddie are two guarantors; insurers include Enact and several rivals.

Rocket describes itself as number one in purchase, refinance, home equity and servicing, citing Inside Mortgage Finance rankings for Q2 2026. We did not find a sourced current-share table for the whole industry.

Originations are fragmented below the top, with banks and independents. Servicing is consolidating, and PennyMac plans to add Cenlar's subservicing business in early 2027. The GSEs remain a two-firm duopoly.

Barriers are meaningful at the top: capital, warehouse lines, investor approvals and, for the GSEs, a federal charter. They are low for small brokers, which is why volume cuts hurt weaker lenders first.

Scale economies show up in servicing cost per loan, technology and funding costs. Rocket reports servicing UPB of $2.0 trillion, and UWM carries $269.8 billion, which is the kind of scale that lowers unit cost.

The product is commoditized on price and differentiated by speed, service and technology. Rocket's gain on sale is 4.31% in direct-to-consumer but 0.70% in Rocket Pro and 0.15% in correspondent, which shows how much brand and channel matter.
Customers (borrowers and brokers) shop on rate, so they hold power in lending. Suppliers such as warehouse banks and the GSEs have power too: the GSEs' pricing and rules set the market's terms.

Revenue follows originations and the servicing book. UWM's Q3 volume was $33.4 billion versus $41.7 billion a year earlier; PennyMac's loan acquisitions and originations were $24.4 billion, down 30% from Q2.
Margins depend on gain on sale, servicing fees and expense control. UWM's gain margin was 124 basis points versus 133 in Q2. PennyMac's production revenue margin was 76 basis points.
Key costs are loan officer pay, marketing, warehouse interest and credit provisions. Fannie's provision was $1.14 billion in Q3 versus $485 million in Q2; Freddie's was $0.8 billion.

Rate sensitivity is very high. The 30-year rate is 7.11% versus 6.24% a year ago, and the MBA's scenarios range from $1.54 trillion of originations with rates 100 basis points higher to $2.64 trillion with rates 100 basis points lower.

The group is exposed to unemployment through delinquencies: Fannie's single-family serious delinquency rate rose to 0.62% from 0.58%. Inflation matters through rates; the FOMC said on 28 Oct 2026 that inflation remains elevated. GDP and house prices affect purchase demand.
It is cyclical, with defensive pieces. Originations swing with rates, while servicing and guarantee income are steadier and rise in value when rates rise. Mortgage insurers are cyclical with credit.

Growth is cyclical, not secular. Rocket's Q3 net income was $709 million against a $124 million loss a year earlier, while PennyMac's net income fell 84% year on year to $29 million. Financials sector Q3 earnings growth was 6.4%.

Gross margins are not a useful measure for lenders. Damodaran's non-bank financial services group (not mortgage-specific, 176 firms) shows a 22.2% net margin and an 18.5% pre-tax operating margin, as of January 2026. Rocket's adjusted EBITDA margin was about 29% of adjusted revenue in Q3 (our calculation).

Return on equity is volatile: PennyMac's annualized ROE was 3% in Q3 versus 18% a year earlier; Enact's adjusted ROE was 12.4%. Damodaran's non-bank financial group shows 28.8% ROE (January 2026), which is inflated by leverage. We did not source ROIC.
Leverage is high. Damodaran's non-bank financial group shows 73% market debt-to-capital and 91% on book. UWM's net non-funding leverage was 1.77x and it plans to cut below 1.5x.

Free cash flow is hard to define for lenders because loans are working capital, so we did not source a comparable figure. Capital return is the practical test: Enact guided to about $600 million of 2026 returns, and PennyMac plans to buy back shares with MSR sale proceeds.
Physical capex is small. Damodaran's non-bank financial group shows capex at 89.7% of depreciation and net capex at 2.4% of sales. The real investment is in servicing rights and technology.

Valuation: the group trades on book value more than earnings. PennyMac said its stock trades at a sizable discount to its $83.85 book value per share. Damodaran's non-bank group has a 16.4x forward P/E versus 27.7x for the whole market in January 2026.

Regulation and policy: the future of the GSEs, including a possible offering, was under study in late 2025 with talk of a roughly $500 billion valuation. We did not find a decision as of November 2026. Capital rules and guarantee fees would reprice the system.
Technology and AI: PennyMac is deploying AI across production workflows to cut costs. We think this lowers cost per loan but also lowers barriers, which pressures margins.
Demographics: household formation and an aging homeowner base shape purchase demand. The MBA projects about 5 million loans a year for the next three years against a peak near 14 million.
Consumer behavior: borrowers with low-rate loans will not refinance or move. The MBA says that with rates of 7% to 7.5% it is very hard to find a reason to refinance.

New competitors: banks lost share (a HousingWire headline says Bank of America's home loan volume fell 12% in Q3), while non-banks consolidate. Fintech lenders and the GSE direct channels are possible entrants.
Geopolitics matters through rates and inflation rather than supply chains. The 10-year Treasury is forecast near 5% and the mortgage spread has widened to about 220 basis points.
Substitutes are renting, cash purchases and government loans; a fall in bond demand would hit the market, as would any removal of the implicit government guarantee.
A lower-rate environment would revive refinancing: the MBA scenario for 100 basis points lower rates is $2.64 trillion of 2027 originations.
Servicing scale and subservicing grow with fee income that is steadier than origination, as PennyMac's Cenlar deal and Rocket's $2.0 trillion book show.
Technology and AI can cut cost per loan and make lenders more profitable once volume returns.
Rates staying above 7% through 2027, with Fed hikes expected, would keep volume near cycle lows.
Credit deterioration is starting to show in GSE and insurer provisions.
Policy risk around the GSEs and the guarantee is unresolved.

Over three to five years this is a rate-driven industry whose profits come increasingly from servicing and guarantees rather than origination. If rates ease, volume has room to recover from about 5 million loans a year, and leaner cost bases at PennyMac and UWM would amplify earnings. If rates stay above 7%, we expect more consolidation, more MSR sales and rising credit costs. We think the GSEs' regulatory outcome is the largest swing factor for the whole system and cannot be forecast from the sources we found.

Mortgage finance is at the weak end of the rate cycle. The 30-year fixed rate averaged 7.11% on 12 Nov 2026 against 6.24% a year earlier, and the 15-year rate was 6.45%. The FOMC held the funds rate at 3.75% to 4% on 28 Oct 2026 by a 10-2 vote, with both dissenters preferring a quarter-point hike, and said inflation remains elevated.

The MBA expects the 10-year Treasury to average 5.1% in Q4 2026, the mortgage spread to stay near 220 basis points, and the Fed to hike by 25 basis points in December and again in Q1 2027. That is the opposite of the easing that refinancing needs.
Currency matters little for a domestic group. The macro hit comes through volume, which the MBA sees at about 5 million loans a year for three years, and through credit if the labor market weakens.

Annual originations are about $2.1 trillion in 2026 and forecast to fall to $1.99 trillion in 2027: purchase $1.42 trillion, up 0.8%, and refinancing $571 billion, down 17%. Purchase activity was about 9% below January levels in the MBA's commentary.

Secular demand rests on household formation and the stock of homes, but the lock-in effect holds many owners with low-rate loans in place. The servicing book is therefore larger and more stable than origination: Rocket services $2.0 trillion for 9.1 million clients, and PennyMac owns $496 billion of servicing, up 6% year on year.

Demand is highly elastic to rates. The MBA's scenarios give $1.54 trillion of 2027 originations with rates 100 basis points higher and $2.64 trillion with rates 100 basis points lower. We see that spread as the best single picture of the industry's sensitivity.

On Porter's five forces, buyer power is high in origination because borrowers and brokers compare rates, and supplier power sits with the GSEs and warehouse banks, whose rules and pricing set the market. Threat of new entrants is moderate: capital and approvals are barriers, but small brokers enter easily. Substitutes are renting and cash buying. Rivalry is intense, which shows in gain on sale ranging from 0.15% in Rocket's correspondent channel to 4.31% in direct-to-consumer.

Concentration is rising in servicing. Rocket gained Mr. Cooper's book, and PennyMac plans to add Cenlar's subservicing business in early 2027. UWM, a wholesale leader, has a servicing portfolio of $269.8 billion and plans to sell $70 billion to $80 billion in MSRs in Q4.
The GSEs' moat is their charter: Fannie guarantees a $4.1 trillion book and Freddie a $3.7 trillion portfolio. We did not find a current industry-wide market share table.

Policy dominates. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac remain in conservatorship, with Fannie's senior preferred liquidation preference at $238 billion and its available CET1 capital at a $30 billion deficit. Freddie has $140.2 billion of Treasury funding available and a $150.4 billion preference.

An offering was under study in late 2025, with officials reportedly envisioning about a $500 billion valuation and a $30 billion raise, and Treasury holding warrants over about 80% of the shares. We found no November 2026 update, so treat it as unresolved.

On the technology side, AI is entering origination and servicing: PennyMac is deploying it across production workflows. On the definitional side, GICS includes servicers and mortgage insurers in the group, so GSE capital standards and insurer capital rules both matter.

Origination is a thin-margin, high-fixed-cost business, so operating leverage is large both ways. PennyMac's production segment lost $7 million pretax in Q3 on a 76 basis-point revenue margin, while servicing earned strongly. Its net income of $29 million compares with $182 million a year ago.

Rocket earned $709 million GAAP, but adjusted net income was $419 million and adjusted EBITDA $748 million, about 29% of adjusted revenue (our calculation). The gap between GAAP and adjusted reflects fair-value marks on servicing and other items.

Returns are uneven. Enact's adjusted ROE was 12.4%; Fannie's return on average required CET1 capital was 11.1%; PennyMac's ROE was 3%. Damodaran's broad non-bank financial group (not mortgage-specific) shows a 22.2% net margin and 28.8% ROE, but 73% market debt-to-capital, so returns are leveraged. Capex is minor at 2.4% of sales for that group.

Earnings are diverging. Fannie's net income rose to $4.2 billion from $4.0 billion in Q2, but its provision rose to $1.1 billion. Freddie earned $3.2 billion, up 17%, on revenue up 19%. Rocket guided Q4 adjusted revenue to $2.1 billion to $2.3 billion, below Q3's $2.57 billion.

For the lenders, we think the key is 2027 volume. The MBA expects originations to fall 5% and refinancing 17%. PennyMac says mortgage demand will stay subdued and has taken action to cut annualized expenses by $160 million by Q1 2027. UWM returned to a $212.5 million profit after a Q2 loss driven by hedging.

We could not source a consensus EPS table for this sub-industry. At the sector level, FactSet shows Financials Q3 blended earnings growth of 6.4% against 31.4% for the S&P 500. Our read is that consensus for the lenders is more exposed to a rate downside than the GSEs, but we have no sourced estimates to test that.

We could not find a sourced sub-industry forward P/E. The Financials sector trades at 15.0x forward earnings against 17.7x for the S&P 500; XLF shows a 16.5x P/E and 2.50x price to book on 11 Nov 2026.

Damodaran's non-bank financial group had a 16.4x forward P/E in January 2026 versus 27.7x for the whole market, but this is not mortgage-specific. Mortgage lenders are better read on book value: PennyMac says its stock trades at a sizable discount to $83.85 of book value per share.

Fannie and Freddie trade over the counter, and the late-2025 reports of a roughly $500 billion IPO valuation compared with a market value of about $20 billion at that time. We read that gap as the market's discount for conservatorship risk, not a forecast of earnings.

None of this group is large in the main Financials ETF. XLF's top ten holdings, as of 11 Nov 2026, are Berkshire, JPMorgan, Visa, Mastercard and large banks and brokers, with total fund assets of $54.2 billion across 76 holdings. Mortgage names are not in the top ten.
XLF returned 9.66% year to date and 22.30% over one year to 31 Oct 2026. We did not find sourced short-interest or flow data for the mortgage names.

Corporate actions are a signal: PennyMac plans to repurchase shares and cut debt using $490 million of MSR sale proceeds; UWM plans a $1.65 billion preferred package led by Oaktree and a $400 million rights offering to cut debt; Enact bought back about $118 million in Q3.

Mortgage REITs just had a bruising third quarter. A jump in long-term rates and wider mortgage spreads cut book value per share by 11.4% at Annaly, 16.9% at AGNC and 15.4% at Dynex, and credit-focused Starwood and Blackstone Mortgage Trust booked large loan-loss charges. Earnings available for distribution still covered dividends at Annaly, but fell short at Starwood. The 30-year mortgage rate was 7.18% on 5 Nov, below its early-October 7.4% peak. The sector ETF REM is down 17.1% year to date. We read the group as a leveraged bet on spreads, now repricing after a drawdown.

Mortgage REITs own loans and mortgage bonds rather than buildings. Most borrow short-term money and buy longer-term mortgage assets, earning the gap between what the assets yield and what the borrowing costs. As REITs they pay out almost all taxable income, so they are bought for dividends. Two families sit here: residential names such as Annaly and AGNC that mainly hold government-backed mortgage bonds, and commercial lenders such as Starwood and Blackstone Mortgage Trust that make loans on offices, apartments and other property. Owners of physical property sit in the Real Estate sector's equity REIT groups, and banks sit in Financials.

Agency mortgage bonds: Bonds backed by home loans and guaranteed by Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac or Ginnie Mae. Credit risk is low, so returns come from the spread over Treasuries, amplified by borrowing. e.g. AGNC, Annaly's Agency group, Dynex, ARMOUR

Residential credit: Home loans and bonds with no government guarantee, so the owner takes the risk of borrowers not paying in exchange for higher yield. e.g. Annaly's Onslow Bay securitizations, Chimera, MFA

Mortgage servicing rights: The right to collect payments on a home loan and keep a fee. These gain value when rates rise and loans repay more slowly, which offsets losses on bonds. e.g. Rithm's Newrez, Annaly's MSR group

Commercial real estate loans: Floating-rate loans to owners of offices, apartments, hotels and industrial property, often held on balance sheet and funded with debt. e.g. Starwood Property Trust, Blackstone Mortgage Trust, Ladder

Origination and asset management: Some names also make new loans, sell them, or manage money for outside investors and earn fees. e.g. Rithm's Newrez and Genesis Capital, Starwood's servicing and infrastructure lending

Mortgage spreads: When the extra yield investors demand rises, agency bond prices fall and book value drops, even with hedges. When it narrows, book value recovers. It is the single largest driver of residential names.
Interest-rate level and volatility: Big, fast moves in long-term yields make hedging harder and widen spreads. Calm markets let a levered portfolio earn its carry.
Funding costs: Repo rates follow the Fed's short-term rate. Higher funding costs shrink the gap between asset yield and borrowing cost.
Prepayment speeds: Lower mortgage rates speed refinancing, which shortens the life of bonds bought at a premium and reduces income. Higher rates slow it.
Commercial real estate credit: Property values, rents and refinancing access decide whether loans repay. Losses appear as reserves, impairments and dividend cuts.
Equity issuance and share price versus book: Names trading above book can sell shares and add assets without diluting book value. Trading below book blocks that growth and may prompt buybacks.
Government housing policy: Decisions on how much Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac buy, and on the future of the agencies, change mortgage demand and spreads.
Book value per share: Net assets divided by shares. Because mortgage REITs hold marked-to-market securities, book value moves with markets, and the share price is often quoted as a multiple of it.
Economic return: The change in book value per share plus dividends paid, as a share of starting book value. It is the cleanest quarterly scorecard.
Agency MBS: Mortgage-backed securities guaranteed by a US government agency or a government-sponsored enterprise, so investors bear rate and prepayment risk but little default risk.
Mortgage spread: The extra yield on mortgage bonds over Treasuries or swaps. When it widens, existing bonds fall in price and book value drops.
Repo (repurchase agreement): Short-term secured borrowing in which the REIT pledges bonds as collateral. It is the main funding for agency names and has to be rolled over every few weeks.
Leverage: Debt relative to equity. Higher leverage magnifies both gains and losses on book value.
Prepayment: Homeowners paying off loans early, usually when they refinance or move. Faster prepayment on bonds bought above par cuts yield.
Earnings available for distribution (EAD): A non-GAAP profit measure that strips out unrealized market swings. Managements use it to judge whether the dividend is covered.
Distributable earnings: The commercial lenders' version of EAD, adjusted for items like loan-loss provisions and realized gains. Dividend coverage is tested against it.
CECL reserve: An accounting provision for expected loan losses booked up front. A big increase hits GAAP income even before a loan is sold or foreclosed.
TBA: To-be-announced forward market for agency bonds. Firms use it to buy or sell mortgage exposure for future delivery without funding it on balance sheet.
Hedge ratio: The share of interest-rate risk offset with swaps or Treasury futures. Hedging cuts rate risk but not the risk of mortgage spreads widening.
Mortgage spreads and long-term rates drive book value, and the 10-year Treasury yield was 4.84% on 5 Nov after topping 5.30% in early October.
Two Fed officials dissented in favour of a rate hike on 28 Oct, so a hawkish turn would pressure funding costs and hedges again.
Federal housing agencies were authorized in January to buy up to $225 billion of mortgage bonds each, a possible support for spreads that analysts questioned.
Commercial-property credit remains the weak link: Starwood booked a $336.6M provision and Blackstone Mortgage Trust took reserves on six newly impaired loans.
Dividend coverage is thin outside agency names: Starwood's distributable earnings of $0.31 were below its $0.48 dividend.
Annaly Capital Management, AGNC Investment, Starwood Property Trust, Rithm Capital, Blackstone Mortgage Trust, Dynex Capital, ARMOUR Residential REIT, Ladder Capital

The main revenue is net interest income: interest on mortgage assets minus the cost of borrowing and hedging. Annaly describes earning the spread between asset yield and borrowing cost. In Q3 2026 its average asset yield was 5.58% and its cost of interest-bearing liabilities 4.34%, a net interest spread of 1.24%. Rithm and Starwood add servicing, origination and fee businesses.

Customers are not consumers but borrowers and capital markets. Residential names buy loans or bonds created by lenders and agencies, while commercial lenders such as Blackstone Mortgage Trust lend to property owners. Shareholders are mostly income investors; REM's trailing distribution yield was 11.39%. Rithm's Newrez originates loans and Genesis made $1.5B of transition loans in Q3.

The principal cost is funding. Annaly had $85.5B of repurchase agreements at 30 Sep 2026, with a weighted average of 30 days to maturity. Interest is followed by hedging costs, management or compensation expense, and credit-loss provisions. Starwood's Q3 provision was $336.6M.

Pricing power is minimal in agency bonds, which trade at market spreads, and slightly greater in credit, servicing and origination, where underwriting skill, sourcing and scale matter. Management cannot set the asset yield. In our view, the differentiator is the ability to buy cheaply when spreads widen and fund at low cost, so scale in repo and securitization is the closest thing to pricing power.

Assets are mortgage bonds, loans and servicing rights; liabilities are mostly repo, securitization debt and unsecured notes. Annaly's $106.5B portfolio was 86% agency by market value ($91.8B), with $10.4B of residential credit and $4.3B of servicing rights. Starwood's commercial lending portfolio was a record $17.8B. AGNC's was $94.4B at fair value.

The group is asset-light in the sense of no plants or stores, yet balance-sheet intensive: it needs equity and funding rather than capital spending. Annaly had 212 employees at the end of 2025. Growth is financed by issuing shares, and AGNC raised $992M through at-the-market sales in Q3.

We did not find a sourced estimate of total sub-industry revenue or assets. As a size marker, REM, which tracks the FTSE Nareit All Mortgage Capped index, held 30 companies and $439.8M of assets at 9 Nov 2026. Annaly's non-affiliate market value was about $12.1B in mid-2025. The ETF's year-to-date return was -17.11%.

The main segments are agency mortgage bonds (Annaly, AGNC, Dynex, ARMOUR), residential credit and servicing (Rithm, Annaly's credit and MSR groups), and commercial real estate lending (Starwood, Blackstone Mortgage Trust, Ladder). REM's top holdings were Annaly 21.73%, AGNC 15.37% and Starwood 6.88% at 30 Sep 2026.

These companies sit between homeowners or property owners, who borrow, and investors who buy mortgage bonds. Suppliers are lenders, the agencies Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and Ginnie Mae, and repo dealers. Annaly's OBX program issued 29 deals backed by $15.2B of whole loans in 2025.

The industry's current form is the legacy of the financial crisis. Agency guarantees, central-bank bond buying and tighter bank capital rules pushed mortgage risk toward REITs and funds. A recent policy turn: in January 2026 the FHFA raised the cap on each government-sponsored enterprise's mortgage-bond holdings from $40B to $225B.

Geography is almost entirely the United States, since the assets are US home loans, US agency bonds and mainly US commercial property. The mortgage rate benchmark is the Freddie Mac survey, which stood at 7.18% on 5 Nov 2026. We did not find a regional split of holdings.

We did not find a sourced count of listed mortgage REITs; REM holds 30. Annaly lists its competitors as financial institutions, institutional investors, other lenders, government entities and other REITs. The competitive set also includes banks, insurers, hedge funds and the housing agencies themselves.

By REM's weights at 30 Sep 2026, the leaders are Annaly (21.73%), AGNC (15.37%), Starwood (6.88%), Ellington Financial (4.57%), Dynex (4.53%), Rithm (4.52%), ARMOUR (4.44%) and Blackstone Mortgage Trust (4.23%). These are ETF weights, which reflect capped market value, not market share of mortgages.

The group is concentrated at the top among agency names and fragmented below. The top two holdings make up 37.10% of REM, and the top 15 make up 84.35%. Against a $13 trillion mortgage market, even the largest firms hold a small fraction.

Barriers are modest in capital terms but real in funding. A new REIT must raise equity, secure repo lines and meet REIT and Investment Company Act tests. Established firms have access to dozens of counterparties and securitization programs, such as Annaly's 101 OBX deals since 2018.

Scale helps with funding terms, hedging costs and securitization access, and with the cost base. Annaly ran with 212 employees at end-2025. The advantage does not show up in asset yield, which is set by the market. We found no sourced operating-cost ratios by company.

Agency bonds are close to commodities, since the credit guarantee is the same across issuers. Differentiation comes from portfolio composition, hedging, leverage and, in credit, underwriting and servicing. Rithm's mix of Newrez servicing and lending earned $329.7M of pretax operating income in Q3.

Bargaining power sits with funding providers and the government agencies. Annaly's repo averaged 30 days to maturity, so lenders can reprice or pull funding quickly. The agencies decide how much supply and demand enters the market, as the cap on their purchases shows. Borrowers have little power over the REIT.

Revenue growth follows portfolio size and the net spread. Growth comes mostly from raising equity and adding assets. AGNC sold 97.6M shares for $992M in Q3. Commercial lenders grow through originations and shrink through repayments, as Blackstone Mortgage Trust collected $2.3B.

Operating margin is the net interest spread minus costs. Annaly's net interest margin was 1.54% on a GAAP basis in Q3. Spreads widen when funding costs fall relative to asset yield and compress when funding costs rise or assets prepay. Hedging gains and losses blur reported margins.

Key cost variables are repo rates, hedging costs, prepayment speeds and credit costs. Annaly's economic cost of liabilities was 4.03%. In commercial lending the largest variable is the provision for loan losses: $336.6M at Starwood.

Interest-rate sensitivity is high and cuts several ways. Short rates set funding cost; long rates and volatility set bond prices and prepayment. Annaly's hedge ratio was 100%, yet book value still fell 11.4% as the 30-year mortgage rate reached a three-year high near 7.4%.

GDP, unemployment and inflation matter mostly through rates and credit. The Fed said on 28 Oct that activity was expanding at a strong pace and inflation remained elevated. Starwood's chairman said higher interest costs were hurting borrowers. Commodity prices matter little directly.

The industry is cyclical with a secular income appeal. Book value swings with rates and spreads: Dynex's fell 15.4% in one quarter. Dividends are the attraction, but payouts can be cut when earnings fall short, as when Starwood's distributable earnings of $0.31 trailed its $0.48 dividend.

Earnings are volatile because GAAP results include market-value changes. Annaly lost $1.36 per share in Q3 2026 on GAAP, yet its earnings available for distribution were $0.80, up from $0.79. Rithm earned $0.38 GAAP and $0.55 in earnings available for distribution. Starwood lost $1.08 per share on GAAP.

Gross margin is not meaningful for lenders. Damodaran's January 2026 table for the broad R.E.I.T. industry (190 firms, mostly equity REITs, so not a close match) shows a 58.08% gross margin, 26.37% pre-tax operating margin and 13.23% net margin. A better indicator here is Annaly's 1.24% GAAP net interest spread.

Returns on equity are low and volatile. Damodaran's broad R.E.I.T. group showed a 5.04% return on equity and a price-to-book of 1.99 in January 2026, though that mixes property owners with mortgage REITs. Annaly's annualized GAAP return on average equity was (24.35%) in Q3 2026. ROIC is not a useful measure for lenders.

Leverage is the defining feature. Annaly's economic leverage was 5.9x and GAAP leverage 8.0x at 30 Sep 2026, AGNC's at-risk leverage was 7.9x and Dynex's 9.0x including TBAs. Starwood's equity was $5.84B against roughly $24.3B of debt on a rough calculation.

Free cash flow is not a standard measure because the balance sheet is the business. Cash earnings are tracked as EAD or distributable earnings: $0.80 for Annaly, $0.31 for Starwood, and $0.42 for Blackstone Mortgage Trust before realized items. Dividends declared were $0.75 at Annaly, $0.48 at Starwood and $0.51 at Dynex.

Capital expenditure is negligible. Growth uses equity and debt instead: AGNC raised $992M through at-the-market share sales in Q3 2026. Liquidity is the constraint: AGNC held $6.3B of cash and unencumbered agency bonds.

Valuation is quoted against book value, not earnings. Damodaran's broad REIT price-to-book was 1.99 in January 2026. We did not obtain current price-to-book ratios for the group. REM's trailing yield was 11.39% at 9 Nov 2026.

Regulatory risk centres on housing finance and REIT status. Annaly must distribute at least 90% of REIT taxable income and meet Investment Company Act exemptions, and its 10-K says the cumulative impact of recent policy shifts is unclear. The January 2026 move to lift the agencies' mortgage-bond cap to $225B is one example.

Technology disruption is limited to origination and servicing, where automation affects Rithm's Newrez. We found no sourced evidence on AI affecting the sub-industry. In our view the main technology effect is in analytics and hedging rather than a threat to the business model.

Demographics matter through household formation and mortgage demand. We did not find sourced demographic data for this group. The more immediate effect is that high rates keep fewer homeowners moving, which slows prepayments: the 30-year rate was 7.18%, against 6.22% a year earlier.

Changing consumer behavior shows up in mortgage demand and lender volume. We found no sourced origination volumes for the group. Rate-lock effects and the choice between renting and owning affect the pipeline. Investor behaviour matters too: REM saw $69M of outflows year to date.

New competitors include banks returning to mortgage bonds, hedge funds and the housing agencies, which can buy bonds directly. The agencies' retained-portfolio caps were raised to $225B each, and analysts questioned whether they have the liquidity to use it. Private credit funds also compete with commercial mortgage REITs, in our view.

Geopolitical shocks flow through rates. The 10-year Treasury yield was 3.97% before the US war with Iran began in late February and exceeded 5.30% in early October. Supply chains matter little, but sanctions, energy prices and inflation expectations affect bond yields and the Fed.

Substitutes exist for income investors, including bonds, credit funds and bank deposits. A mortgage REIT's dividend is only as safe as its earnings. Starwood's distributable earnings did not cover its dividend in Q3, and Blackstone Mortgage Trust took reserves against six impaired loans of about $800M.
Wider spreads raise forward returns on new agency purchases, as Dynex's chief executive called the market a compelling forward opportunity.
If long-term yields keep easing from 5.30% in early October toward the 4.84% of 5 Nov, book values could recover.
Commercial lenders are collecting repayments and shrinking watch lists, with Blackstone Mortgage Trust's watch list the lowest since 2019.
Bigger agency purchases could narrow spreads if the January 2026 authority is used.
A hawkish Fed could push long rates and spreads higher again, as two Fed officials already wanted a hike.
More office and property loan losses could force further reserves and dividend pressure at credit lenders.
High leverage of 7.9x to 9.0x leaves agency names exposed to funding squeezes.
Housing finance policy is unsettled, and analysts questioned the agencies' ability to execute large purchases.

We think the next three to five years depend on whether rates settle. The third quarter showed how fast leveraged mortgage portfolios can lose book value when spreads widen, with declines of 11.4% to 16.9% in the agency names. The same widening raises the yield on new purchases, which management teams are citing as a reason to stay invested. Credit lenders face a longer clean-up in commercial property, where reserves and sales continue. Policy is the wild card, since agency purchases and any changes to the housing agencies would alter mortgage demand. We would watch dividend coverage and book value trends rather than headline yields.

The group is in a rate shock rather than a recession. The Fed held its target range at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 Oct 2026 by a 10 to 2 vote, with both dissenters preferring a quarter-point rise, and said activity was expanding at a strong pace while inflation remained elevated. That is a difficult mix for levered holders of fixed-rate assets.

Long rates did the damage. The 10-year Treasury yield surged above 5.30% in early October, against 3.97% before the war with Iran began in late February, and stood at 4.84% on 5 Nov. The Freddie Mac 30-year rate peaked near 7.4%, a nearly three-year high, and eased to 7.18% by 5 Nov against 6.22% a year earlier.

The hit showed up in Q3 book values: Annaly's fell 11.4% to $17.86, AGNC's tangible book fell $1.45 to $7.13, and Dynex's fell to $10.91 from $12.90. Blackstone Mortgage Trust said the impact of higher rates was largely reflected in its book value. Our read is that the cycle is turning from a shock to a repricing, and a hawkish Fed would reopen the risk.

We did not find a sourced estimate of the addressable market for mortgage REIT capital. The underlying mortgage market is large: a news report put it at about $13 trillion. Mortgage REITs are a small part of that, funding a slice of agency and credit risk.

Demand for the product is demand for income. REM's trailing 12-month distribution yield was 11.39%, but the fund returned -17.11% year to date and -13.32% over one year, against +8.36% over three years. Flows were -$69M year to date. This is a cyclical, rate-sensitive demand pool.

On the asset side, high mortgage rates cap lending. The 30-year rate was 7.18% on 5 Nov, up from 6.22% a year earlier. Rithm's Newrez and Genesis Capital still originated, with Genesis making $1.5B of transition loans in Q3. Annaly's residential credit group has been growing securitization volume, with 29 OBX deals in 2025.

Demographics matter only indirectly. Household formation and the pace of home sales set new mortgage supply, and we found no sourced demographic data for this group. Our view is that the long-term prospects depend more on rates and on housing policy than on population growth.

Applying Porter's five forces, rivalry is high in agency bonds, where products are interchangeable and the largest names compete for the same assets. Annaly and AGNC together make up 37.10% of REM's weights. Buyer power, in the sense of borrowers, is low, but supplier power is high: repo lenders can reprice quickly, with Annaly's repo averaging 30 days to maturity.

The threat of new entrants is moderate. Capital is available, but a new REIT must manage REIT distribution rules, the Investment Company Act and funding access. The threat of substitutes comes from banks, insurers, hedge funds and the housing agencies themselves, which can buy mortgage bonds directly, as FHFA's January 2026 cap change allows.

Moats are thin in agency bonds and stronger where origination, servicing or underwriting skills matter. Rithm's Newrez produced $329.7M of pretax operating income in Q3, and Starwood has a record $17.8B commercial lending book alongside servicing and infrastructure lending. Our read is that scale and diversified franchises explain who recovers fastest.
Concentration is high at the top: REM's top 15 holdings made up 84.35% of the fund at 30 Sep 2026. We found no sourced share of the overall mortgage market for these firms.

Regulation shapes the business model. Annaly distributes at least 90% of REIT taxable income and must fit within an exemption from the Investment Company Act. It has also claimed relief from CFTC commodity pool operator rules for mortgage REITs. Housing finance is political: in January 2026 the FHFA raised each agency's limit on mortgage-bond holdings from $40B to $225B, against a $200B target.

The policy has critics. Analysts said neither Fannie Mae nor Freddie Mac appeared to have the liquidity to buy $225B, and economists called it a short-lived boost. FHFA's director said purchases would not exceed $200B. Treasury's $450B cap still applies. For REITs, agency buying competes for supply but can narrow spreads.

The Fed is the other key policy actor. Its 28 Oct statement said inflation was elevated and two members wanted to raise rates. Geopolitics enters through energy and rates: the 10-year yield was 3.97% before the war with Iran began in late February and topped 5.30% in early October.

Technology is a modest factor. It affects loan origination and servicing at Rithm and hedging and analytics across the group. We found no sourced evidence of AI disrupting the business, and we do not claim any.

Reported margins are not comparable with other industries. The core measure is net interest spread: Annaly earned 5.58% on assets and paid 4.34% on liabilities, a 1.24% spread, and a net interest margin of 1.54% in Q3 2026. Leverage of 5.9x economic and 8.0x GAAP turns that thin spread into a mid-single-digit return on equity before market-value moves.

Damodaran's January 2026 data for the broad R.E.I.T. group (190 firms) show a 26.37% pre-tax operating margin and 13.23% net margin, and a 5.04% return on equity. That group includes property-owning REITs, so it is not a clean read for mortgage REITs. We did not find ROIC or free cash flow, which are not standard for lenders.

Operating leverage is limited because the business is spread capture. Costs are small in dollars, since Annaly runs on 212 employees, but credit losses can swamp it. Starwood's $336.6M provision produced a $389.7M GAAP loss against distributable earnings of $116.8M. Blackstone Mortgage Trust posted a $327.6M net loss but $0.42 of distributable earnings.

Capital intensity is about equity, not capex. Growth needs equity issuance and funding lines: AGNC raised $992M in Q3. Dividends are then paid out of distributable earnings, which is why REIT payout rules make equity markets essential.

Underlying earnings held up better than GAAP. Annaly's earnings available for distribution were $0.80 per share, up from $0.79, against a GAAP loss of $1.36. Rithm's were $0.55 against GAAP $0.38. AGNC declared a $0.36 dividend against a GAAP loss of $1.17 per share.

Credit lenders are weaker. Starwood's distributable earnings were $0.31 ($0.41 before realized losses) against a $0.48 dividend. Blackstone Mortgage Trust's were $0.42 per share before realized items on a GAAP loss of $1.95. Credit costs are the swing factor here.

Consensus figures for this group were not publicly available in the sources we opened, and we do not estimate them. FactSet's 6 Nov report covers the S&P 500, where Financials reported 6.4% blended Q3 earnings growth, but it does not isolate this sub-industry.

Our view: the next two quarters will be set by book value recovery and dividend decisions. Management commentary is constructive on new asset returns. We think dividend cuts are the likeliest negative surprise at credit names, since coverage is already below 100% at Starwood.

Mortgage REITs are valued on price to book and yield rather than forward earnings. We did not obtain current prices or price-to-book multiples for the bellwethers, so we do not rank them. REM's trailing yield was 11.39% at 9 Nov 2026, and the fund fell 17.11% year to date.

For context, Damodaran's January 2026 price-to-book for the broad R.E.I.T. industry was 1.99, with a 5.04% return on equity. That figure includes equity REITs and predates the Q3 drawdown, so we would not apply it to mortgage REITs. A useful rule is that a company's price-to-book should relate to its sustainable return on equity.

Market-wide, FactSet shows the S&P 500's forward 12-month P/E at 17.7 on 5 Nov 2026, below its 5-year average of 19.8 and 10-year average of 19.1, with Financials at 15.0 and among the lowest of the sectors. These are not this group's multiples.

Book value after the drawdown is lower and, if spreads hold, so is the base on which dividends are earned. Management teams argue that wider spreads create attractive entry yields. Our read is that the group looks priced for continued risk, but the sources we opened do not give prices, so we do not say it is cheap or dear.

Momentum is negative and flows are weak. REM returned -17.11% year to date and -13.32% over one year, with $69M of outflows year to date, and assets of $439.82M at 9 Nov 2026. It returned +8.36% over three years and -27.52% over five.

Ownership is concentrated in a few names. REM held Annaly at 21.73%, AGNC at 15.37% and Starwood at 6.88% at 30 Sep 2026. The ETF holds 30 securities and costs 0.48% a year. This is ETF evidence from one fund; we did not obtain institutional holdings, short interest or breadth data.

Companies themselves are active in the market. Starwood repurchased a record $108M of its shares in Q3, while AGNC issued 97.6M shares for $992M. Firms buy back stock when below book and issue when above, so the mix signals relative valuation versus book value at each company.
Market-wide context is cautious: FactSet shows Financials with the lowest forward P/E among sectors at 15.0. We make no claim about positioning beyond what these sources show.

Large drugmakers just reported a strong third quarter, but the profit pool is concentrating in obesity and immunology. Eli Lilly's revenue rose 39% to $24.4B on volume up 53% and realized prices down 15%. AbbVie grew 10.3% and Merck 5%, while Pfizer was flat and Teva fell 2% as generics slipped. Policy is the swing factor: Section 232 tariffs of up to 100% are waived for firms with pricing deals, and 26 drugmakers covering about 90% of branded US sales had signed by September. Patent expiries put roughly $300B of revenue at risk by 2030.

These companies discover, make and sell prescription medicines. Branded firms such as Lilly, Merck and Pfizer earn most of their profit from patented drugs sold to patients through insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, hospitals and governments; when a patent expires, cheaper generics or biosimilars arrive and sales drop. Generic makers such as Teva compete on price and volume. GICS also places animal health, such as Zoetis, here. Biotechnology companies sit in a separate sub-industry, Life Sciences Tools and Services firms supply the labs, and drug distributors and pharmacies sit in Health Care Distributors and Retail.

Branded small-molecule drugs: Pills made by chemical synthesis and protected by patents, usually for 20 years from filing. They carry high margins until generics arrive. e.g. Eliquis, Rinvoq, Jardiance

Biologics and antibodies: Large molecules made in living cells, often injected or infused. Copies called biosimilars are harder to make than generics, so erosion is slower. e.g. Keytruda, Skyrizi, Humira
Obesity and diabetes injectables: GLP-1 type drugs that mimic a gut hormone to lower blood sugar and body weight. They have become the largest new category by sales. e.g. Mounjaro, Zepbound, Wegovy
Vaccines: Products that prevent infection. Demand depends on public health recommendations and government purchasing. e.g. Gardasil, Prevnar, Comirnaty
Generics and biosimilars: Copies of drugs whose patents have expired, sold at a fraction of the brand price to many buyers. e.g. Teva generics and biosimilars
Animal health: Medicines and vaccines for pets and farm animals, sold through veterinarians and distributors. e.g. Zoetis Simparica and Librela, Merck Animal Health
Volume of new blockbusters: A successful launch, such as an obesity or immunology drug, can add billions in sales within two years because the cost of making the next unit is low.
Patent expiries: Revenue on a lost-exclusivity drug can fall fast once copies arrive, so analysts track the calendar of expiries for each large company.
Net price: Discounts, rebates, government price rules and tariffs set the price the company actually keeps. A fall in realized price shows up directly in revenue and margin.
R&D productivity: Spending on trials and acquired research assets drives cost. Approvals and trial results decide whether that spending is rewarded.
Policy and regulation: FDA approvals, Medicare negotiation, tariffs and pricing deals change which drugs can be sold and at what price.
Acquisitions and licensing: Large companies buy or license assets to refill their pipelines. Deals bring one-off charges and later, if successful, new revenue.
Currency and public purchasing: Foreign sales are converted into dollars, and vaccine or antiviral sales swing with government orders.
Patent cliff: The sharp revenue drop when a blockbuster loses patent protection and cheaper copies enter. It is the central risk for branded drugmakers.
Loss of exclusivity (LOE): The date a drug can legally face generic or biosimilar competition. Analysts model each major product's LOE date.
Biosimilar: A close copy of a biologic drug. It needs more testing than a generic pill, so entry is slower and discounts are smaller.
Gross-to-net: The gap between a drug's list price and what the company keeps after rebates and discounts paid to insurers and middlemen. A widening gap cuts reported revenue.
Pharmacy benefit manager (PBM): An intermediary that negotiates rebates with drugmakers for insurers and decides which drugs are covered. It gives buyers leverage over price.
Most favored nation (MFN) pricing: A policy that ties US prices to the lowest prices paid in other rich countries. It is the main US pricing threat to branded drug margins.
Acquired IPR&D: The cost of buying unfinished research assets, expensed immediately. It can cut reported profit by a lot in the quarter of a deal, so firms show adjusted figures as well.
Pipeline: Drugs in clinical trials. Investors value a company partly on how likely the pipeline is to replace sales lost to patent expiry.
Phase 3 trial: The final, large human trial before approval. Results often move share prices sharply.
Orphan drug: A drug for a rare disease, which gets extra market protection and, under US law, some exemption from Medicare price negotiation.
Medicare negotiation: A US program under the Inflation Reduction Act in which the government sets prices for selected high-spend drugs.
Operational growth: Growth excluding currency swings. Companies quote it to show underlying demand.
Lilly's Q3 realized price fell 15% as volume rose 53%, so the obesity franchise is growing on volume while price erodes.
Novo Nordisk plans to cut US list prices on Wegovy by about 50% and Ozempic by about 35% from 1 January, which it expects to pressure 2027 cash flow.
Section 232 tariffs took effect from 31 Jul 2026 for named firms and 29 Sep 2026 for the rest, with relief for companies that sign MFN pricing deals; generics are exempt for now.
Bristol Myers' Eliquis and Opdivo and Merck's Keytruda, which is over half of Merck's sales, are the largest franchises facing expiry and biosimilar erosion.
Medicare's third negotiation cycle covers 15 drugs, including Part B drugs for the first time, with negotiated prices applying from 2028.
Eli Lilly, Johnson & Johnson, AbbVie, Merck, Pfizer, Bristol Myers Squibb, Zoetis, Teva

Revenue comes mainly from patented prescription drugs. In Q3 2026 Lilly's Mounjaro and Zepbound together made $16.1B of $24.4B revenue, AbbVie's Skyrizi and Rinvoq $8.5B of $17.4B and Merck's Keytruda family $8.6B of $18.1B. Generic makers like Teva and animal-health firms like Zoetis add different models.

Customers are not usually patients directly. Drugs are bought through wholesalers, pharmacies, hospitals, insurers and governments, with Medicare and Medicaid central in the US. Lilly said its US price fell mainly on Zepbound after rebate and discount adjustments, which shows how payers shape net revenue. Merck cited lower US public-sector purchasing for Vaxneuvance.

The main costs are research and development, marketing and administration, and manufacturing. Lilly spent $4.25B on R&D, 17% of Q3 revenue, AbbVie's adjusted R&D was 13.9% of revenue, and Pfizer guides 2026 adjusted R&D to $10.8B to $11.8B and SI&A to $12.5B to $13.5B. Cost of goods is small for branded drugs, shown by Lilly's 84.4% non-GAAP gross margin.

Pricing power comes from patents, clinical evidence and a lack of substitutes, and is checked by payers and governments. It is strongest for new drugs with no close rival and weakest after expiry. Lilly's realized price fell 15% worldwide in Q3 while volume rose 53%, which in our view shows pricing power being traded for volume in a competitive, price-scrutinised category.

Major assets are patents, a drug pipeline, plants and acquired intangibles; major liabilities are debt, rebate accruals and litigation. J&J booked a $5.5B pre-tax litigation-related adjustment for its proposed talc resolution in Q3. Teva carried net debt of $12.6B on 30 Sep 2026. We did not obtain balance sheets for the others.

Branded pharma is moderately capital-intensive: heavy on R&D, light on fixed assets relative to revenue. Damodaran's January 2026 US data show net capital spending of only 1.12% of revenue for the industry. Biologics plants and the new US onshoring push raise spending, but these are small beside R&D.

We did not find a single sourced global market-size figure. The best available gauge is company revenue: the companies in this brief guide to 2026 revenue of about $101.2B at J&J (including MedTech), $91B to $92B at Lilly, $66.8B to $67.3B at Merck, $62B to $64B at Pfizer and $49.75B to $50.25B at Bristol Myers.

The main segments are immunology, oncology, obesity and diabetes, cardiovascular, vaccines, neuroscience, generics and animal health. In Q3, obesity and diabetes led growth at Lilly, immunology at AbbVie, oncology and vaccines at Merck, and generics fell 16% at Teva while its branded drugs grew 33%. Animal health made up $1.7B at Merck and $2.4B at Zoetis.

Drugmakers sit between research suppliers (biotechs, contract labs, universities) and buyers (insurers, governments, hospitals). Large firms refill pipelines by buying or licensing: Pfizer took a $650M charge for an Innovent deal and Lilly booked $4.2B of acquired IPR&D in Q3. Regulators, led by the FDA, gate every launch.

The industry has shifted from small-molecule blockbusters to biologics and now to obesity drugs, with costs of replacing expiring products pushing firms toward deals. FDA's list shows 48 novel drug approvals in 2026 so far, the latest on 9 Nov. Drug pricing has become a trade and political issue, with tariffs tied to pricing agreements.

Sales are concentrated in the US, where prices are highest, but growth outside it is large. Lilly's Q3 US revenue rose 34% to $15.1B and non-US revenue 47% to $9.3B, helped by China. We did not find a sourced table of production by country; of the companies here, Novo is Danish and Teva Israeli, and the rest are US-based.

A small number of large companies dominate by value, with hundreds of smaller ones. Damodaran's US industry data count 228 firms in Drugs (Pharmaceutical). The group is broader than this sub-industry, but the top names in this brief hold most of the sales.

The leaders by size on 2026 revenue guidance are J&J (including MedTech), Lilly, AbbVie, Merck, Pfizer and Bristol Myers. Novo Nordisk is Lilly's main obesity rival, guiding to adjusted sales growth of -2% to +2% against Lilly's 39% quarter. We did not find sourced market-share tables across the industry.

The industry is concentrated at the top for branded drugs and fragmented in generics. Teva's US generic revenue of $718M fell 39% in Q3, which in our view reflects crowded generic markets and price pressure. Branded firms compete drug by drug within each disease area rather than across the whole industry.

Barriers to entry are very high: patents, years of clinical trials, FDA approval, manufacturing know-how and the cost of discovery. Drugs reaching approval still face payer scrutiny. The FDA approved 48 novel drugs in 2026 through 9 Nov, so new entrants are possible but a small number of drugs.

Scale helps with trial funding, global launches and negotiating with payers. AbbVie earned a 48.7% adjusted operating margin and Lilly's operating income was $8.6B on $24.4B of revenue. Smaller firms often sell or license drugs to the large firms to reach scale, as the Innovent deal shows.

Branded drugs are differentiated, but within a class they can be close substitutes: payers decide formulary placement. Generics are commodities. Lilly's price decline of 15% and Novo's planned list-price cuts suggest competition is turning even the newest classes toward price.

Bargaining power sits with payers and governments for large drugs, and with drugmakers for new drugs with no rival. Medicare will set prices for 15 more drugs from 2028, and MFN deals plus tariffs tie access to concessions. Suppliers have little power because the key inputs are mostly the companies' own intellectual property.

Revenue growth is driven by new products and volume, offset by price and patent expiry. Lilly's volume rose 53% and price fell 15%. J&J's Innovative Medicine grew 7.7% despite Stelara's loss of exclusivity, which cut about 690 basis points from operational growth. AbbVie's Humira fell 31.2% while Skyrizi grew 22.7%.

Operating margin depends on gross margin, R&D intensity and acquired-research charges. AbbVie's adjusted operating margin was 48.7%, Teva's non-GAAP operating margin 31.7% and Lilly's reported operating income 35% of revenue (our arithmetic from $8.6B on $24.4B). Damodaran's industry pre-tax operating margin is 29.5%.

Key costs are R&D, acquired IPR&D, sales and marketing and tax. Bristol Myers' non-GAAP EPS fell to $1.35 from $1.63 as acquired IPRD cost $0.58 a share. Lilly's $4.57 per share of IPR&D charges offset a $4.07 rise in underlying EPS guidance. Tariffs add a new cost for imports without a pricing deal.

Interest rates matter modestly: demand for prescription drugs does not depend on borrowing, but rates affect deal financing and the discount rate on distant pipeline cash flows. Damodaran's data show high multiples on forward earnings of 24.2x, which in our view makes the group sensitive to rate expectations. We did not find a sourced rate-sensitivity estimate for the industry.

Inflation, unemployment, GDP and commodities matter less than for most industries. Demand follows disease burden and insurance coverage, not the cycle, though job losses can reduce coverage. Inflation matters through price controls: the Inflation Reduction Act ties negotiated prices to government rules. We did not find a sourced commodity sensitivity.

Pharma is mainly defensive with secular growth drivers, but not immune. Health Care's blended Q3 earnings growth was 9.3% against 31.4% for the S&P 500, and individual companies swing with patents and trials: Pfizer's revenue was flat as Paxlovid fell 63% and Comirnaty 29%.

Growth varies widely by company. In Q3 2026 revenue rose 39% at Lilly, 10.3% at AbbVie, 7% at Bristol Myers, 5.9% at J&J, 5% at Merck, flat at Pfizer and fell 2% at Teva and 1% at Zoetis. Health Care sector earnings grew 9.3% blended.

Margins are high. Damodaran's January 2026 data give a 29.5% pre-tax operating margin and 26.4% after tax for 228 US firms. Company gross margins are higher: 85.1% adjusted at AbbVie, 84.4% non-GAAP at Lilly and 58.7% non-GAAP at Teva. Zoetis's adjusted net income margin was about 30.1% in Q3, our calculation.

Returns on capital are high. Damodaran gives a 29.3% return on capital and a sales-to-invested-capital ratio of 1.11 for the industry. Goodwill from acquisitions lowers reported returns at acquisitive firms. We did not find a sourced ROE for this sub-industry.

Leverage differs by company. Teva had $16.7B of debt and $4.1B of cash, net debt of $12.6B, on 30 Sep 2026. AbbVie's Q3 net interest expense was $700M GAAP. Pfizer paid $7.3B of dividends in nine months and guides to no 2026 buybacks. We did not obtain debt balances for the other companies.

Free cash flow is large at the leaders but uneven. Teva guides 2026 free cash flow of $2.1B to $2.4B on $16.7B to $17.0B of revenue. Novo Nordisk raised its 2026 free cash flow guidance to DKK 60B to 70B. We did not obtain free cash flow figures for Lilly, J&J or Merck.

Capital spending is low relative to revenue. Damodaran's industry net capital spending was 1.12% of revenue, with working capital at 38.3% of revenue. The heaviest outflows are R&D and deals rather than plants, though onshoring pledges tied to tariff relief may raise factory spending.

Multiples are high on current earnings. Damodaran's January 2026 US data give forward P/E 24.2x, trailing P/E 55.7x and EV/EBITDA of 15.3x for profitable firms (18.6x for all). EV/EBIT was 20.3x on the same basis. The trailing figure is inflated by depressed earnings at some firms, in our view.

Regulation is the largest risk. Section 232 tariffs reach 100% on patented imports for companies without pricing or onshoring deals. Medicare negotiation will cover 15 more drugs from 2028, including the first Part B drugs. MFN agreements covering about 90% of the branded market are in place, but terms are confidential. The proposed Medicare MFN models were not confirmed as final in the source we opened.

We did not find a sourced figure on AI's effect on drug-development productivity, so we make no claim. The clearer technological shift is new drug formats: Merck's under-the-skin Keytruda Qlex had $830M of Q3 sales, and Novo's Wegovy pill passed 8 million US prescriptions.

Demographics are a support rather than a risk. Ageing populations raise demand for cancer, heart and immunology drugs, and Merck, J&J and AbbVie all report growth in cancer and immunology. The risk is that payers, facing the cost of ageing, push harder on price, as the Medicare programme shows.

Consumer behavior is shifting toward direct-to-patient channels and cash-pay obesity drugs. The Pfizer MFN agreement was announced alongside TrumpRx, a government site for discounted direct purchases, and Novo's Wegovy pill passed 8 million US prescriptions after launch.

New competitors include Chinese-licensed drugs and, in obesity, Novo plus a wave of entrants. Lilly's non-US price fell 29% mainly because Mounjaro joined China's national reimbursement list. Pfizer's Innovent deal is an example of licensing from Asia.

Geopolitical and supply-chain risk is now concrete. Tariffs apply at 15% for EU, Japanese, South Korean and Swiss goods under trade deals and at 10% for the UK, with a 100% default for others. Lilly names trade protection measures as a risk but did not quantify a tariff cost.

Substitutes are mainly generics and biosimilars, plus new drug classes. Pfizer expects a $1.1B 2026 revenue hit from generic and biosimilar competition. Evaluate puts revenue at risk from patent expiries at $300B by 2030. Bristol Myers' Eliquis and Opdivo are among the largest drugs expiring.
Obesity and diabetes demand is still growing fast, with Lilly's Mounjaro and Zepbound up 65% and 49% in Q3.
Immunology franchises keep compounding, with AbbVie's Skyrizi and Rinvoq up 22.7% and 23.9%.
New formats such as subcutaneous Keytruda Qlex can extend franchises past patent expiry.
Pricing deals that exempt companies from tariffs give clearer policy terms for the 26 signatories.
Patent expiries put about $300B of revenue at risk by 2030, with Bristol Myers, Merck and Pfizer the most exposed.
Price erosion is spreading to new classes, with Lilly's realized price down 15% and Novo cutting US list prices.
Medicare negotiation widens to Part B drugs, with 15 more drugs priced from 2028.
Tariffs of up to 100% remain the default for firms without pricing or onshoring deals.

We think the next three to five years split the group into winners and refillers. Lilly, AbbVie and parts of J&J have products growing double digits, while Bristol Myers, Merck and Pfizer must replace large expiring franchises, which is where the Evaluate estimate of $300B at risk bites hardest. Policy has become more predictable for companies that signed pricing deals, but net price pressure continues, as Lilly's 15% fall in realized price shows. Volume growth has so far outrun price cuts, but we would not assume that continues as obesity drugs mature. Deal-making is likely to stay active as firms fill gaps.

Pharmaceuticals are a defensive, policy-driven group rather than a cyclical one, so the macro backdrop matters mainly through the equity market and policy. FactSet's 6 Nov 2026 report shows the S&P 500 forward P/E at 17.7x, the lowest since late 2023. The index is on track for 33.3% calendar-2026 earnings growth. Health Care is growing far slower: its blended Q3 earnings growth is 9.3% against 31.4% for the index, and revenue growth is 6.3%. These are sector figures that include insurers and services.

Policy is the more important input than the rate path. The April 2026 Section 232 proclamation set a 100% default tariff on patented drug imports, 15% for the EU, Japan, South Korea and Switzerland and 10% for the UK, with exemptions for companies that have pricing agreements and for generics. By September, 26 drugmakers covering about 90% of the branded US market had signed such agreements, according to a White House statement cited by Wikipedia. We treat that source with care.

Currency has a modest effect: Merck's worldwide sales grew 5% reported and 4% excluding currency, and Novo's DKK sales grew 6% reported and 4% at constant rates. We found no sourced estimate of how the interest-rate path changes the group's earnings.

Demand rests on disease burden, ageing and new treatments, not the economic cycle. We did not find a sourced estimate of total industry revenue or its growth. The largest firms' 2026 guidance provides a floor on scale: about $101.2B at J&J including MedTech, $91B to $92B at Lilly, and $66.8B to $67.3B at Merck.

Growth is concentrated in a few categories. Lilly's Mounjaro and Zepbound together sold $16.1B in Q3. AbbVie's Skyrizi and Rinvoq reached $8.5B, up from a year earlier by 22.7% and 23.9% respectively. Merck's Keytruda family sold $8.6B and Winrevair rose 93% to $694M. Novo's obesity sales were DKK 26.1B, up 22%, with the Wegovy pill adding DKK 5.4B.

The new-product flow is steady: the FDA lists 48 novel approvals for 2026 as of 9 Nov. Against that, mature categories are shrinking: Pfizer's Paxlovid fell 63% and Comirnaty 29%, and Teva's global generics revenue fell 16%. Animal health shows more mixed demand, with Zoetis companion animal revenue down 5% and livestock up 7%.

Demand is inelastic for needed medicines but elastic for discretionary or high-cost categories, and payers can restrict use. In our view, ageing populations are a durable tailwind, but their effect on revenue is limited by price control rather than patient numbers.

On Porter's five forces, entry barriers are very high, since discovery, trials, FDA approval and manufacturing take years and billions of dollars; the FDA approved 48 novel drugs in 2026 through 9 Nov, a small flow against thousands of candidates. Rivalry is intense within each therapeutic class, as Lilly and Novo show in obesity, where Novo is guiding to flat sales while Lilly grows 39%.

Buyer power is the strongest force. Governments and insurers set coverage and increasingly price: Medicare negotiation extends to 15 more drugs from 2028, and MFN agreements tie prices to other countries. Supplier power is low for the large firms because discovery is largely in-house, but they depend on acquired assets: Lilly booked $4.2B of acquired IPR&D in a quarter.

The threat of substitutes comes from generics, biosimilars and rival classes. Pfizer expects a $1.1B hit in 2026 from generic and biosimilar competition. Evaluate's estimate of $300B at risk by 2030 puts Bristol Myers' gap at about $38B, Merck's at $23B and Pfizer's at $21B, while Lilly has limited exposure.

Moats are patents and clinical data, so they expire. AbbVie shows a company that has replaced a lost franchise: Humira fell 31.2% to $683M while Skyrizi and Rinvoq grew to $8.5B. Generic makers have no moat but scale: Teva's US generic revenue fell 39%. We did not find sourced industry concentration ratios.

Government is the dominant outside force. Politically, the Section 232 proclamation of 2 Apr 2026 imposes tariffs of up to 100% on patented drug imports, effective 31 Jul 2026 for named companies and 29 Sep for others, and waives them for firms with MFN pricing agreements or approved onshoring plans (20%, rising to 100% in April 2030). Generics and several specialty categories, including orphan-only drugs and cell and gene therapies, are exempt for now.

Pricing regulation is moving on two tracks. Medicare's third negotiation cycle named 15 drugs on 27 Jan 2026, including Part B drugs for the first time, with prices applying from 2028; the 2025 budget law widened the orphan-drug exclusion, delaying Keytruda and Opdivo to later cycles. Separately, CMS proposed mandatory Medicare MFN models, and a voluntary Medicaid model had been joined by all states by September 2026, per the source we opened.

FDA remains the gatekeeper and has kept a steady flow, with 48 novel approvals in 2026 through 9 Nov. Technology is changing formats more than the science of approval: Merck's Qlex had $830M of sales in Q3 and Novo's Wegovy pill passed 8 million prescriptions.

The social and legal environment matters too. J&J's Q3 earnings include a special charge for a proposed talc litigation resolution, with a $5.5B pre-tax litigation adjustment. We did not find a sourced assessment of how AI affects drug development and make no claim.

The economics are among the best in the market. Damodaran's January 2026 data for 228 US pharmaceutical firms show a pre-tax operating margin of 29.5%, an after-tax margin of 26.4% and a return on capital of 29.3% on a sales-to-capital ratio of 1.11. Net capital spending is only 1.12% of revenue. These are broad industry averages that include small firms.

Company data show the range. AbbVie's Q3 adjusted gross margin was 85.1% and its adjusted operating margin 48.7%. Lilly's non-GAAP gross margin was 84.4% and its operating income was $8.6B on $24.4B revenue, held down by $4.2B of acquired IPR&D. Teva's non-GAAP operating margin was 31.7%. Zoetis's adjusted net income was $720M on $2.39B of revenue.

Operating leverage is strong when a product scales: Lilly's gross profit rose 40% on revenue up 39%, while R&D rose 23%. It reverses when a franchise expires: AbbVie's Humira dropped 31.2%. Deal charges distort comparisons, as Bristol's non-GAAP EPS fell 17% with a $0.58 charge.

Free cash flow is strong but varies. Teva guides 2026 free cash flow of $2.1B to $2.4B and Novo of DKK 60B to 70B. Pfizer paid $7.3B of dividends in nine months. We did not find a sourced ROE for the sub-industry.

Revisions in Q3 were mostly upward for revenue. Lilly raised 2026 revenue guidance to $91B to $92B from $85B to $87B and lifted underlying EPS by $4.07 at the midpoint, though reported non-GAAP EPS guidance of $35.00 to $36.00 fell slightly because of the Q3 IPR&D charge. Pfizer raised revenue guidance to $62B to $64B and EPS to $2.95 to $3.05. AbbVie raised EPS to $13.95 to $13.99, J&J to $11.05 to $11.15 and Merck narrowed and raised its sales midpoint to $66.8B to $67.3B.

Others were mixed. Bristol Myers raised revenue guidance to $49.75B to $50.25B but set non-GAAP EPS at $6.35 to $6.55, which includes a $0.60 per share acquired-IPRD hit. Teva raised revenue guidance to $16.7B to $17.0B. Zoetis narrowed revenue to $9.22B to $9.32B and raised adjusted EPS to $6.25 to $6.35. Novo raised its outlook to -2% to +2% growth.

At sector level, FactSet shows Health Care blended Q3 earnings growth rising to 9.3% from 5.2% a week earlier, with the sector reporting the largest aggregate positive surprise, +13.7%; Pfizer ($0.87 vs $0.74) and Lilly ($7.48 vs $5.71) were among the largest beats. This is the sector, which includes insurers.

Our view: the headline beats overstate underlying momentum for the older franchises, because growth is narrow. Merck and Pfizer depend on a few products and large expiries are ahead. We did not find consensus 2027 estimates for the group and make no estimate.

We did not obtain a current forward P/E for the group, so we use Damodaran's January 2026 US industry data, which are ten months old. They show a forward P/E of 24.2x for Drugs (Pharmaceutical), a trailing P/E of 55.7x and a PEG ratio of 1.40. EV/EBITDA was 15.3x for firms with positive EBITDA and 18.6x for all firms, with EV/EBIT at 20.3x and 21.1x.

For comparison, FactSet put the S&P 500 forward P/E at 17.7x on 5 Nov 2026, below its 5-year average of 19.8x and 10-year average of 19.1x. If the industry still traded near Damodaran's 24.2x, it would sit at a premium to the market; we cannot confirm that today. We did not find a FactSet Health Care forward P/E in the report text we could read.

Earnings quality complicates multiples. Reported EPS is cut by deal charges (Lilly $4.57 a share, Bristol $0.58), and some earnings come from products with known expiry dates. In our view, a high multiple on today's earnings embeds the assumption that pipelines replace lost sales.

Free cash flow yields cannot be computed without current prices, which we did not obtain for individual names. Teva guides free cash flow of $2.1B to $2.4B. We make no claim about whether the group is cheap or expensive against its own 10-year history because we did not find that series.

The best positioning data are for the broader Health Care sector, not the sub-industry. The Health Care Select Sector SPDR (XLV) held $50.49B of assets, closed at $188.85 on 13 Nov 2026 and returned 25.64% over one year. Its top holdings are Eli Lilly at 16.75%, J&J at 10.04%, AbbVie at 7.64%, Merck at 5.32% and Pfizer at 2.41%. Pharmaceutical names make up a large share of the 64 holdings but the fund also holds insurers and device makers.

Concentration is notable: Lilly alone is 16.75% of the fund, so sector performance is tied to the obesity trade. Lilly's Q3 revenue beat of $24.40B against $22.58B expected was a leading contributor to Health Care's revenue upgrade.

Capital returns support the group: Pfizer paid $7.3B of dividends in nine months and expects no 2026 buybacks. We did not obtain short-interest, institutional flow or breadth data for pharmaceuticals, nor the group's year-to-date performance against the S&P 500, and make no claim about them.

Medical device makers just reported a split third quarter. Intuitive Surgical grew revenue 22% on 14% more da Vinci procedures, Edwards raised its 2026 sales outlook to about 11.5% growth and Abbott's devices rose 7.8% on a comparable basis. Boston Scientific grew only 1.5% after a cybersecurity incident and cut its outlook, and Stryker cut its guidance on weaker hip and knee demand. Tariffs are a cost but a manageable one at Intuitive, about 0.9% of revenue. The iShares device ETF trades on a 33.6 P/E and is down 7.2% this year.

These companies design, make and sell the physical tools of medicine: surgical robots, heart valves and stents, joint implants, monitors, imaging systems and glucose sensors. Customers are mainly hospitals and surgery centres, which buy through purchasing groups, and patients paying through insurers or Medicare. Revenue comes from selling devices, from single-use supplies used in every procedure, and from service contracts. GICS keeps diagnostics tools and supplies in other sub-industries, and drug companies, distributors and hospital operators sit elsewhere in Health Care.

Surgical robotics: Robotic systems that let surgeons operate through small incisions. The maker sells or leases the system, then earns on instruments and accessories used in each procedure. e.g. Intuitive da Vinci and Ion, Medtronic Hugo, Stryker Mako

Cardiovascular devices: Implants and catheters that treat the heart and blood vessels, including heart valves, stents, pacemakers and ablation tools for abnormal rhythms. e.g. Edwards TAVR valves, Boston Scientific Watchman, Medtronic and Abbott electrophysiology

Orthopaedic implants: Hip, knee, shoulder and spine implants plus the instruments and navigation used to place them, used mostly in planned operations. e.g. Stryker knees and hips, Zimmer Biomet, Medtronic spine

Diabetes technology: Continuous glucose monitors and insulin pumps worn by patients, sold as recurring sensors and supplies. e.g. Abbott FreeStyle Libre, Medtronic diabetes (being separated as MiniMed)
Neuromodulation: Implanted devices that send electrical pulses to nerves to treat chronic pain or movement disorders. e.g. Boston Scientific neuromodulation, Abbott neuromodulation, Medtronic
Monitoring and imaging equipment: Bedside monitors, ultrasound and other equipment sold to hospitals as capital purchases or through leases. e.g. Masimo pulse oximetry, hospital monitors
Procedure volumes: More operations mean more instruments, implants and supplies sold. Elective procedures such as knee replacement can be delayed when patients lose insurance or worry about costs.
New product cycles: A new generation such as a next-model robot or ablation system lifts both volume and price per procedure, until competitors catch up.
Reimbursement and hospital budgets: Medicare rates and hospital finances set what buyers can pay. Tighter budgets slow capital purchases and delay adoption of new devices.
Tariffs and supply chains: Many companies manufacture in Mexico, Ireland, Germany and Asia. Duties on imports raise cost of goods and press gross margin unless prices rise.
Regulation and recalls: FDA decisions open or close markets, and recalls or cybersecurity problems can stop shipments for weeks.
Acquisitions: Large firms buy fast-growing niches, lifting growth and adding debt and integration risk.
Currency: Sales abroad are translated into dollars, so a weaker dollar adds to reported growth and a stronger one subtracts.
Procedure volume: The number of operations or interventions performed using a company's devices. It is the main demand gauge because most revenue is used up in each procedure.
Installed base: The count of systems already placed in hospitals. A larger base means more future sales of instruments and service.
Razor and blade model: Selling or leasing the system at a modest margin and earning repeatedly on the single-use instruments and accessories that go with it.
Recurring revenue: Revenue from supplies, instruments and service that repeats with each procedure or contract, rather than one-off equipment sales.
Organic growth: Sales growth excluding acquisitions, divestitures and currency moves. It is the cleanest measure of underlying demand.
Premarket approval (PMA): The FDA's most demanding review route, for high-risk implants such as heart valves. Clinical data are required, which keeps rivals out.
510(k) clearance: An FDA route for devices shown to be substantially equivalent to one already on the market. It is faster and cheaper than PMA.
Reimbursement: What Medicare and insurers pay for a procedure or device. A new device needs adequate coverage to be adopted.
Pass-through payment: Extra temporary Medicare payment to hospitals for a new, costly device, so they can afford to adopt it.
Pulsed field ablation (PFA): A newer way to treat atrial fibrillation using electrical pulses rather than heat or cold. It is a major growth area for several leaders.
TAVR: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement: a heart valve implanted through a catheter without open-heart surgery.
Value-based or volume-based procurement: Government or hospital buying that sets a low price in exchange for volume, as China has done for some devices. It cuts prices.
Medtronic reports fiscal second-quarter results on 24 Nov 2026, the next read on cardiac ablation after 88% growth in that line last quarter.
The Commerce Department's Section 232 investigation into medical device imports was still open at 28 Oct 2026 with no published decision, so new tariffs remain possible.
Boston Scientific guided Q4 net sales down 1% to 3% after an August cybersecurity incident, so recovery in the first half of 2027 is the test.
